summary: Exhaustively audit the cfi-defect-repository for latent operational time bombs

findings.title: Anthropic monthly spend cap starves the pipeline mid-month and the run still reports ok=True — the $2/day cap does not protect against it, and it already happened once (2026-07-13)
findings.evidence: run.py:128-131 (`_api_limit_hit`: 'reached your specified api usage limits' — with the docstring noting 424 good articles were WARN'd through it on 2026-07-13) and the break-out handlers at run.py:177-181, 201-204 and auto_review.py:141-143. The daily budget is $1.95 (config_settings.json:73), i.e. ~$60.45 over a 31-day month — if the Anthropic console monthly limit is below that (or the key is shared with other CFI automations like the SC-tracker curation), the monthly cap trips before month-end. Crucially, when the limit hits, cmd_process/auto_review just `break` — no exception propagates, `ok` stays True (run.py:391-405), so no GitHub failure email fires and /qa shows a green run that extracted nothing.
findings.failure_scenario: Mid-month the monthly cap trips. Collect keeps ingesting hundreds of articles/day into status 'fetched'; extraction and adjudication process zero; auto-publish stops; the map freezes with green telemetry. When the month resets, the backlog can only drain at $1.95/day while new articles keep arriving, so it may never catch up — and the defect-vocabulary-first sort (run.py:147-150) means the behaviour-crash tail that feeds the >=3-in-6-months escalation counter is what silently rots.
findings.fix: 1) Set the Anthropic console monthly limit to at least 31 x daily budget + headroom (>= $70) and put this pipeline on a dedicated API key so other projects' spend cannot trip it. 2) When _api_limit_hit fires, write a distinct flag into pipeline_run stage_stats (e.g. api_monthly_limit_hit=true) and send the existing Slack webhook a one-line alert — the plumbing already exists in watch.notify(). 3) Show fetched-backlog size on /qa so a growing queue is visible.

verdict.reason: All cited evidence verified line-for-line: _api_limit_hit (run.py:128-131) documents the cap actually tripping 2026-07-13 (day 13 of the month), all three handlers break silently, stage() only flips ok on exceptions so ok=True/exit 0/green /qa/no GH email is exact, and $1.95/day (config_settings.json:73) ≈ $60/month makes a mid-month trip recurrent unless the console cap was raised. The code corroborates further: health.py's publishing_alive freeze-detector passes at spend<$0.10 (the zero-spend cap signature), and the min_extracted_last_run check that would directly catch it is declared in DEFAULTS but never implemented in collect_checks(). Only mitigation is the queue_depth≥4000 Slack alert — days-to-weeks delayed, contingent on an optional secret, and misattributing the cause to the daily budget.

findings.title: Geocode cache is ephemeral in CI: data/ is gitignored and daily.yml never persists it, so every run re-buys the same geocoding calls from cold
findings.evidence: geocode.py:36 `CACHE_PATH = ROOT / "data" / "geocode_cache.json"`. `.gitignore` contains `data/` (verified: `git ls-files data/` is empty; local cache has 258 entries but is untracked). .github/workflows/daily.yml has no actions/cache step, no artifact upload, no commit-back — a fresh `actions/checkout` starts every run with NO cache file. The cache therefore only memoizes within one run. Bonus defect: `_save_cache()` (geocode.py:57-59) rewrites the entire JSON file after EVERY cache miss (geocode.py:80-81, 118-119) — O(cache_size) disk write per request, quadratic I/O within a run as the cache grows.
findings.failure_scenario: Every negative result (failed lookups, exactly the ones finding #1 retries daily) is re-purchased every day forever: the cached `None` that would have made retries free is thrown away at run end. At retry-set saturation this is ~6-12k cold requests/day: Mapbox free tier (100k/month) is exhausted in ~10-15 days of each month → overage billing or 429s that silently degrade every geocode to Nominatim-only, whose 1.1s/call rate limit converts the whole load into ~2-3h of wall-clock sleep per run. Timeline: cost/latency grows linearly starting now, becomes run-threatening at the same 4-8 month horizon as finding #1.
findings.fix: Persist the cache across runs: either (a) actions/cache keyed on a static key with restore-keys (`path: data/geocode_cache.json`), or (b) move the cache into Postgres (`geocode_cache(key text primary key, result jsonb, created_at)` — it already has a DB) with a 90-day TTL delete in the hygiene stage so IT doesn't grow forever. Also fix _save_cache to write once at stage end (atexit or explicit flush in cmd_geocode) instead of per miss.

verdict.reason: Every evidence claim verified against the repo: cache lives at data/geocode_cache.json (geocode.py:36), data/ is gitignored with zero tracked files, and daily.yml (checkout/setup-python/install/run/deploy) has no actions/cache, artifact, or commit-back step — CI starts every run with an empty cache and discards it. The scenario mechanism is confirmed and slightly understated: the main geocode pass (run.py:263, 'where geom is null', limit 1000, no status filter) retries never-geocodable incidents forever, and the Mapbox rescue pass (run.py:296-305) re-geocodes all sub-0.6 items in auto/needs_human every run — needs_human never drains because auto_review.py only processes 'auto'. cmd_daily uses limit=1000 for both passes, so saturation matches the claimed 6-12k requests/day (2000 items x 3-6 ladder variants), exceeding Mapbox's 100k/month free tier, with failed items also paying Nominatim's 1.1s sleep per variant (~2h added against a 330-min timeout where collect already takes ~2h). Local cache shows 119 cached-None negative results that CI re-buys daily. Timeline is plausible: ~16% of geocodes land below the publish bar per the run log, giving saturation within the claimed 4-8 months; cost grows linearly starting now, and the dual cron trigger doubles cold cost on failure days. The O(cache_size)-write-per-miss bonus defect is also confirmed (geocode.py:57-59, 80-81, 118-119) but is minor on ephemeral runners.

findings.title: Articles stuck in processing_status 'new' accumulate forever — unresolved Google News links, GDELT rows, and empty fetches are dead rows nothing retries or prunes
findings.evidence: 'new' is written on three paths: run.py:57 (unresolved gnews links — `args.no_fetch or not it.resolved` means the body is never fetched and the stored url is the google redirector), run.py:70 (fetched but empty clean_text), run.py:96-103 (ALL GDELT items — inserted with clean_text=None and never fetched). The only consumer of articles is `articles_by_status("fetched")` (run.py:143); no stage ever selects status='new' for retry, despite rss.py:8-9 promising "Unresolved links keep the google URL and are flagged so fetch can retry later" — that retry does not exist anywhere (grepped: no transition from 'new' except at initial insert). health.py:20 alerts at 15,000 but is monitoring only; there is no pruner (the only DELETEs in the codebase are dedup merges).
findings.failure_scenario: Every gnewsdecoder failure (rate-limited batchexecute calls fail routinely) and every GDELT run adds permanently-dead rows. At plausibly 100+/day the 15,000 alert fires in ~4-5 months and then fires every day forever with no remediation path. The rows inflate seen_url/near_duplicate scan cost (finding #6), table/index bloat, and — because unresolved rows store the google URL — the same article can be inserted a second time under its publisher URL after a later successful resolve, so they aren't even useful as dedup keys.
findings.fix: Two-part: (1) add a retry stage that picks `status='new' and url like '%news.google.com%' and created_at > now()-interval '7 days'` and re-attempts resolve+fetch (fulfilling rss.py's promise), flipping to fetched/failed; (2) add to the hygiene stage a hard prune: delete (or collapse to url-only tombstones) 'new' rows older than 30 days — RSS collection window is 2 days, so a 30-day-old 'new' row can never be re-surfaced by a feed and its URL-dedup value is nil for google redirector URLs.

verdict.reason: Every code claim verifies: 'new' is written at run.py:57 (unresolved gnews links, google URL stored), run.py:70 (empty clean_text), and run.py:96-103 (GDELT, never fetched); the sole consumer is articles_by_status("fetched") at run.py:143; no code path selects or transitions status='new' (the retry promised at rss.py:8-9 is unimplemented); the only DELETEs are incident dedup merges; health.py new_stuck_alert=15000 is monitoring only. Production DB confirms and exceeds the scenario: 10,016 rows stuck in 'new' (43% of source_article, largest status class), none ever transitioned since 4 Jul, accruing at ~626/day over the last 7 days — 6x the finding's estimate — so the 15,000 alert fires in ~8 days (not 4-5 months) and then daily forever with no remediation path. Minor softenings: GDELT is not part of the daily cron (manual runs only), and per-row storage is small so DB-size impact is modest; but the perpetual-alert, dead-row-majority, and silent article-loss consequences are all real.

findings.title: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY death is invisible: pipeline stays green while producing nothing
findings.evidence: run.py:128-131 special-cases only the literal string 'reached your specified api usage limits'; every OTHER Anthropic exception (401 after key rotation, org disabled, changed error wording) is caught per-article at run.py:176-183 (relevance: WARN + continue, article stays 'fetched') and run.py:201-207 (extraction: WARN + article marked 'failed' permanently). auto_review.py:140-146 has the same per-item catch. The health watchdog cannot catch it either: health.py's 'publishing_alive' check is `pub > 0 or spend < 0.10` — a dead key means $0 spend, so the check PASSES; and `min_extracted_last_run` is defined in DEFAULTS (health.py:23) but never referenced in collect_checks(). In-code precedent: run.py comment '2026-07-13: 424 good articles were WARN'd through it'.
findings.failure_scenario: Key is rotated in the Anthropic console (or the org hits a differently-worded limit). Next morning's run: relevance 401s on every article, stage completes, ok=True in pipeline_run, GitHub Actions green, no email. Articles pile up as 'fetched'; any that reach extraction get status 'failed' and are permanently dropped from the queue. Discovery comes only when the fetched backlog crosses the 4000 queue_depth threshold (~2+ weeks at current volume) — and that alert is delivered via the Slack webhook, which can itself be dead (finding 7). Map freezes, exactly like the 11-14 Jul incident, but with zero red signal.
findings.fix: (1) In cmd_process and auto_review.run, treat anthropic.AuthenticationError / PermissionDeniedError as run-fatal: re-raise so the stage records FAILED, ok=False, SystemExit(1), GitHub failure email. (2) Actually implement the min_extracted_last_run check in health.py collect_checks (it is dead config today). (3) Add a validity probe to check-secrets.yml: GET https://api.anthropic.com/v1/models with the key; non-200 exits non-zero so GitHub emails fire independent of Slack. Run it on a monthly cron, not just workflow_dispatch.

verdict.reason: Every evidence claim verified in code. run.py:128-131 special-cases only the literal 'reached your specified api usage limits' string, so a 401/auth error after key rotation matches nothing and falls into the per-article catches: relevance (run.py:176-183) WARNs and leaves articles 'fetched'; extraction (run.py:201-207) marks them 'failed', permanently dropping them from the fetched-only queue; auto_review.py:138-146 has the identical per-item swallow. The watchdog is blind by construction: min_extracted_last_run is defined in health.py DEFAULTS (line 21, with a comment naming this exact failure mode) but grep confirms it is never referenced in collect_checks() or anywhere else; publishing_alive (health.py:59) is 'pub > 0 or spend < 0.10' and llmcost only accrues on successful calls, so a dead key gives $0 spend and the check passes. cmd_daily's stage() only fails on raised exceptions, so the run ends ok=True/exit 0, GitHub Actions stays green (daily.yml has no notification step; the 15:00 retry only triggers on failed runs), and pipeline_run.stage_stats records process:'done' — failed counts exist only in stdout logs. First automated signal is queue_depth at 4000 fetched, weeks away and delivered solely via the shared Slack webhook. Plausible well within 6 months: key rotation/org changes are routine, error wording is provider-controlled, and the repo documents a precedent (2026-07-13: 424 articles WARN'd through a limit error). High severity is appropriate for weeks of silent zero-output on a publicly cited live map.

findings.title: REVIEW_USERS fails OPEN: losing the Render env var silently removes all auth from the publish console
findings.evidence: review/app.py:40-41 — `if not users: return "reviewer:local"` — the no-auth 'open local mode' is triggered purely by REVIEW_USERS being unset, and runs identically on the public Render URL. render.yaml declares REVIEW_USERS with `sync: false`, meaning it must be hand-entered every time the service is (re)created from the blueprint.
findings.failure_scenario: Render blueprint re-sync, service recreation, region move, or a teammate deploying a fresh instance skips the manual env-var step. The app boots normally with zero authentication on a public onrender.com URL. Anyone who finds it can Approve (which explicitly OVERRIDES the confidence gate and publishes to the public dashboard), Reject, Edit, or Merge incidents. The audit log attributes everything to 'reviewer:local', so tampering is indistinguishable from legitimate local dev. Nothing errors, nothing alerts — this credential's 'rotation failure' mode is not an outage but an open door.
findings.fix: Fail closed in production: in reviewer(), `if not users and os.environ.get("RENDER"): raise HTTPException(503, "REVIEW_USERS not configured")` (Render sets RENDER=true automatically). Keep open mode only behind an explicit REVIEW_ALLOW_OPEN=1 for localhost.

verdict.reason: Verified end-to-end: review/app.py:37-40 returns "reviewer:local" with no auth whenever REVIEW_USERS is unset, empty, or malformed (no colon); render.yaml declares REVIEW_USERS sync:false and starts uvicorn on 0.0.0.0 on a public Render URL; approve sets verification_status='reviewed' which migrations/004 public_incident view publishes unconditionally (gate bypass confirmed in gate.py:9-10); audit log records who="reviewer:local", indistinguishable from local dev. No RENDER-env or fail-closed safeguard exists. The trigger requires a deployment mistake, but the failure is silent (app works perfectly without the var, unlike DATABASE_URL which fails loudly), undetectable, and a blank or typo'd value at Render's blueprint prompt also opens it — realistic within 6 months for a small team on a one-click-redeploy blueprint.

findings.title: Daily LLM budget ($1.95) processes ~250-300 articles/day vs ~430-650/day entering the queue — the fetched backlog structurally diverges
findings.evidence: config/config_settings.json sets llm_budget_usd_per_day=1.95 with extraction_budget_share=0.5 (llmcost.py:47, run.py:158). Measured from the production DB: backlog of processing_status='fetched' was 0 for every day through 12 Jul, then 79/429/373/422/456/1399 per collection day from 13 Jul — 3,158 queued today, oldest from 13 Jul. Runs 11-17 all hit the cap ($1.90-$2.01 spent). Throughput at cap: ~80 sonnet extractions + ~80 sonnet adjudications + ~150-200 haiku relevance calls/day (irrelevant 1,470 + extracted 1,249 lifetime over ~9 processing days ≈ 275/day). Net deficit ~350-450 articles/day at 3 states.
findings.failure_scenario: The queue never converges. Publication latency is already ~6 days (oldest queued = 13 Jul) and grows ~1.3 days per elapsed day at 146 districts. At 722 districts inflow scales ~4.9x to ~2,100-3,200 fetched/day while throughput stays ~275/day (budget-fixed): backlog grows ~+2,500/day (~75k/month), and the map's 'daily' data becomes weeks then months stale within the first month of national rollout. The divergence began 13 Jul (the day the Anthropic monthly limit stopped processing, spend $0.35) and the pipeline has never caught up since — empirical proof the system has no catch-up capacity.
findings.fix: Make the budget scale with the queue: either raise llm_budget_usd_per_day to at least inflow x unit cost (~$6/day at 3 states, ~$25-30/day national), or cut inflow before it costs money — tighten prefilter.passes() so more articles die pre-LLM, and skip fetching near-duplicate/aggregator tiers at collect. Add a convergence alarm: fail the run (or Slack-alert) when count(fetched) grows N days in a row.

verdict.reason: Every element verified against code and production DB. Config sets llm_budget_usd_per_day=1.95 with extraction_budget_share=0.5 (config_settings.json:73-74); llmcost.over() + run.py:160-164 hard-stop processing at the cap with articles left 'fetched' and no catch-up mechanism. DB confirms the exact claimed backlog (3,158 fetched; 79/429/373/422/456/1399 per day from 13 Jul; zero backlog before), runs 11-17 at cap ($1.90-$2.01 except the $0.35 API-limit day that started the divergence), and inflow ~430-490/day vs net queue clearance of ~30-125/day since 13 Jul — the queue has never shrunk on any full-budget day, so the deficit is empirically proven, and is actually worse than the finding's ~275/day throughput estimate. health.py's queue_depth_alert (4000, will trip within days) shows the author anticipated this exact mode ('diverging queue means the daily budget can't keep up') but it only alerts — it does not add capacity. The 722-district extrapolation (~4.9x inflow on a fixed budget) is arithmetic, not speculation, and divergence is already live at 3 states. Mitigations (zero-cost prefilter, defect-first ordering, dedup) shape which articles are dropped but cannot close the gap.

findings.title: daily.yml timeout-minutes 330 (and GitHub's 6-hour job hard cap) vs ~52s/district collect: the single-job design breaks between ~340 and ~380 districts — national (722) is impossible in this architecture
findings.evidence: daily.yml:16 'timeout-minutes: 330' with the comment 'collect alone can take ~2h' at 146 districts (~49-52s/district: run 17 total 8,582s; runs 10-16 9,000-12,100s). Collect is strictly sequential per district with a 2.0s per-domain fetch delay (run.py:407-412, cmd_daily hardcodes delay=2.0) plus one seen_url round-trip per RSS item (store.py:130-133). 722 districts x 52s = 37,544s = 10.4h for collect alone. GitHub-hosted runners hard-cap any job at 6 hours, so even raising timeout-minutes cannot reach national scale. Run #18 (18 Jul) already shows the kill pattern: pipeline_run row has finished_at=NULL, ok=NULL, no stage_stats, zero incidents created that day, 1,399 articles stranded in 'fetched'.
findings.failure_scenario: At ~340 districts (330 min minus ~40 min of post-collect stages at 52s/district), the job is timeout-killed mid-collect: Python dies without stage guards firing, so process/geocode/auto_review/export never run; the deploy step's !cancelled() condition is false on job timeout, so the site is not redeployed; the 15:00 IST retry hits the identical wall. Result at national scale: every scheduled run killed daily, map permanently frozen, backlog and raw_html compounding, with pipeline_run rows silently unfinished (the run-18 signature).
findings.fix: Shard collect: a matrix job per state (or per ~50-district batch) writing to the same DB, followed by a single dependent process/export job. Alternatively parallelize collect_district with a worker pool (the 2s politeness delay is per-domain, so 10-20 concurrent districts is safe) to bring 722 districts under ~1h. Also make cmd_daily write a partial pipeline_run update after each stage so a killed run leaves telemetry.

verdict.reason: All key evidence verified: daily.yml:16 timeout comment exact; collect is strictly sequential with hardcoded delay=2.0 (run.py:407-412) and per-item seen_url round-trips (store.py:130-133); GitHub API shows full runs at 146 districts take 8,518-12,286s and live DB confirms run #17 = 8,582s (~50s/district); pipeline_run #18 confirmed stranded (finished_at/ok/stage_stats all NULL), proving hard kills bypass stage guards and the deploy step. 722 districts × ~50s ≈ 10h collect alone exceeds GitHub-hosted 6h job hard cap, so national scale is impossible in this single-job design, with break point ~320-350 districts. Growth from 38→146 districts in 10 days plus an explicitly national 722-district config makes crossing ~340 within 6 months plausible. Minor caveat: run #18's actual cause was the 18 Jul disk-full outage, not a timeout, but it correctly demonstrates the identical unclean-death signature a timeout kill would leave.

findings.title: 10,016 articles (about 60% of daily collection) sit in processing_status='new' forever — no stage ever fetches or retries them
findings.evidence: Articles whose Google News URL fails to resolve (it.resolved false) or whose fetch throws are inserted with status 'new' (run.py:57, run.py:70, run.py:78-80). The only consumer of the queue is cmd_process via articles_by_status('fetched', ...) (run.py:143); grep confirms nothing anywhere transitions 'new' → 'fetched'. Production DB: 10,016 rows in 'new' vs 1,249 ever extracted; per-day: 766-975 of ~1,400-1,800 collected articles land in 'new' and stay there (e.g. 17 Jul: 920 of 1,584).
findings.failure_scenario: The registry's effective coverage is ~40% of what collect finds, silently — no error, no metric on the dashboard (only health.py counts it). Regional/vernacular outlets with slow or flaky resolution are disproportionately dropped, biasing the map toward well-behaved national domains — the opposite of the 90%-regional design goal. At 722 districts this is ~4,000-5,000 articles/day silently discarded.
findings.fix: Add a refetch pass to cmd_daily: retry 'new' rows up to K times over N days (articles_by_status('new', limit) → fetch_article → promote to 'fetched' or demote to 'failed' after K attempts), and surface the new-count in pipeline_run stage_stats so the drop rate is visible.

verdict.reason: Verified in code and production DB. run.py:58 only fetches when it.resolved; unresolved/failed items insert with status 'new' (run.py:57,70,78-81), and the sole queue consumer is articles_by_status('fetched') (run.py:143) — repo-wide grep confirms no code ever transitions 'new' anywhere. rss.py:8-9 docstring even promises unresolved links are 'flagged so fetch can retry later', but that retry stage was never built — a design gap, not intent. DB numbers match exactly: 10,016 'new' (9,268 of them unresolved news.google.com URLs) vs 1,249 extracted; 17 Jul lost 920/1,584. Last 10 days: 8 of 10 days lost 50-70% of collection. Two tempering facts: (a) loss is intermittent Google rate-limiting — 9 Jul and 18 Jul lost only ~4-5%, proving these URLs ARE resolvable on retry, which makes the missing retry pass more costly, not less; (b) health.py does count the pile ('new_stuck_alert' at 15,000) but the threshold is uncrossed, it only warns, and its comment mislabels the rows 'unresolvable'. The vernacular-bias sub-claim is plausible but unverified (resolution failure isn't obviously outlet-correlated). Core claim — majority of collection silently discarded with no recovery path, scaling linearly with district count — stands. Keeping high: 50-70% silent coverage loss on most days is existential for a coverage-credibility product, and a cheap retry pass would recover most of it.

findings.title: Deploy step runs even when export never produced data — a pre-export failure replaces the live site with a dataless build
findings.evidence: daily.yml:74 deploy condition is `steps.guard.outputs.go == 'yes' && !cancelled()` (runs after ANY prior step failure). web/public/data/{hotspots.geojson,incidents.json,meta.json} are NOT in git (`.gitignore` `data/` matches web/public/data; `git ls-files web/public` lists only SVGs), so the comment 'the site deploys whatever is committed' is wrong — only export creates the files on the runner. Additionally run.py:396-405 stage() catches only Exception, but cmd_collect raises SystemExit at run.py:113 (BaseException) which aborts cmd_daily BEFORE export while deploy still runs; same for failures in 'Install dependencies' or 'Sync configs' steps, or export itself crashing (run.py stage guard marks it FAILED, but the data dir stays absent/partial).
findings.failure_scenario: Any failure before export completes (pip install flake, load_configs.py error, a bad state name in config making cmd_collect raise SystemExit, DB pooler blip during export, missing 'priority_tiers' row -> TypeError on cur.fetchone()[0]) -> Vercel builds the Vite app with no /data directory and deploys it to production. App.jsx fetch('data/meta.json').json() throws -> blank/broken public dashboard. The workflow email says 'run failed' but not 'prod is now broken', and with daily morning-retry failure emails already habituating the team, the broken public site can sit a day or more until an external visitor notices — the worst kind of failure for a credibility-first public registry.
findings.fix: Gate deploy on export having actually produced data: in the deploy step, before `vercel deploy`, run `test -s public/data/meta.json && test -s public/data/hotspots.geojson || (echo 'no export output — refusing to deploy' && exit 1)`. Better: have export write a `_export_ok` marker with counts, and add a pre-deploy sanity check that fetches the LIVE site's meta.json and refuses to deploy if hotspot/incident counts drop >20% or files are missing (protects against empty-view regressions too). Also change run.py stage() to catch BaseException-except-KeyboardInterrupt, or wrap cmd_collect's SystemExit into a normal exception, so config errors can't skip the guard chain.

verdict.reason: Verified in full. daily.yml:74 deploys on `go == 'yes' && !cancelled()`, running after any prior step failure. web/public/data/{hotspots.geojson,incidents.json,meta.json} are untracked (bare `data/` in .gitignore matches at any depth; `git ls-files web/public` returns only 3 SVGs), so the code comment at run.py:394 ("the site deploys whatever is committed") is wrong — the runner's checkout has no data dir and only export_public creates it. run.py:396-405 stage() catches only `Exception`; cmd_collect's `raise SystemExit("no matching district/state...")` escapes it and aborts cmd_daily before stage("export") at line 462. Stronger unguarded path the finding understated: cmd_daily opens a DB connection and inserts the pipeline_run row at run.py:386-390 BEFORE any stage guard, so a pooler blip or Supabase quota event there aborts pre-export while deploy still fires; likewise failures in the 'Install dependencies' or 'Sync configs' steps. web/package.json build is plain `vite build`, which succeeds with no data dir, so Vercel ships a dataless bundle to prod. App.jsx:29-33 has no .catch(), so `data` stays null and line 73 renders "Loading registry…" permanently — the public dashboard is bricked, not merely stale. No file-existence precondition on the deploy step anywhere, and the daily self-healing-retry failure emails habituate the team to ignore the only signal. Realistic within 6 months given the repo's own history of Supabase quota and API-limit incidents.

findings.title: Collect can fail 100% (RSS blocked or Google-News decoder dead) and the run still exits 0 with a green check and a freshly-dated site
findings.evidence: run.py:44-47 catches every rss.collect exception per query ('WARN rss failed', errors++, continue) — all queries failing still returns normally. Worse: rss.py:96-100 swallows all googlenewsdecoder exceptions -> resolved=False -> run.py:58 `if not args.no_fetch and it.resolved` skips the body fetch -> article inserted with processing_status='new', and cmd_process only reads status 'fetched' (run.py:143) — 'new' rows are never revisited by anything. So if Google changes the batchexecute format (googlenewsdecoder breaks regularly) or rate-limits GH runner IPs with 429s (raise_for_status at rss.py:110, caught upstream), the pipeline ingests nothing processable while every stage reports success. stage() at run.py:399 stores `fn() or "done"` and _collect returns None, so pipeline_run.stage_stats records the string 'done' — the zero counts exist only in Actions stdout.
findings.failure_scenario: Google blocks/changes format on day X. Every day after: 0 fetched articles, process/geocode/auto_review no-op on empty input, export rewrites identical JSON with a fresh generated_at, Vercel deploys 'successfully', the site footer says 'Updated 19 Jul' — the freshness indicator actively lies. GitHub shows green runs. Nobody is emailed. Time to notice: 1-3 weeks, and only if a human happens to observe that public counts/queue have been static.
findings.fix: At the end of cmd_daily, evaluate canaries and flip ok=False (which already guarantees SystemExit(1) -> failure email) when: collect total new==0, or fetched-status inserts==0, across all states. Make _collect/cmd_process/cmd_geocode return their stats dicts so pipeline_run.stage_stats holds real counts. Add 'articles ingested today' + 'newest public incident date' to /qa and to a one-line daily Slack digest (reuse SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL). Also stop dead-ending unresolved articles: retry 'new' rows with a resolve+fetch pass on subsequent days, and count resolved==0 as its own canary (detects decoder death separately from RSS death).

verdict.reason:
Confirmed on all counts, and the obvious refutation (the health watchdog) fails to cover it.

Evidence chain verified in /Users/a39002/Documents/Claude/crashfree-infra-repo:
- pipeline/run.py:44-47 — per-query `except Exception: print WARN; errors++; continue`. All queries failing still returns stats normally; cmd_collect returns, stage() records success.
- pipeline/collectors/rss.py:99-100 — bare `except Exception: pass` around gnewsdecoder, leaving out=(google_url, False) i.e. resolved=False.
- run.py:58 — `if not args.no_fetch and it.resolved` skips the body fetch, so the row keeps processing_status='new' (set at run.py:57).
- run.py:143 — cmd_process only pulls `store.articles_by_status("fetched", ...)`. Grepped store.py: no other caller reads 'new'. Those rows are terminal-by-accident, never revisited.
- run.py:399 — `stats[name] = fn() or "done"`; _collect (run.py:407) returns None, so pipeline_run.stage_stats literally records the string "done" for collect. Zero counts exist only in Actions stdout.
- scripts/export_public.py:94 — `"generated_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()`, rewritten unconditionally. The freshness stamp is decoupled from whether anything was ingested.
- .github/workflows/daily.yml — Vercel deploy step runs even when stages fail; run exits non-zero only if a stage raised, which this path never does.

The decisive part: pipeline/processing/health.py DOES exist as a watchdog with Slack alerting, but it does not catch this.
1. `min_extracted_last_run: 1` is declared in DEFAULTS (health.py:21) with the comment "0 extractions = budget/API/collect silently dead" — and is never referenced in collect_checks(). The check written for precisely this failure was never implemented.
2. The nearest live check, `publishing_alive` (health.py:59), is `pub > 0 or spend < 0.10`. A total collect failure means no new 'fetched' rows, so once the existing backlog drains, LLM spend goes to ~0, the `spend < 0.10` clause is satisfied, and the check reports OK. The condition is inverted relative to this failure mode: the deader the pipeline, the greener the check.
3. config/config_settings.json has no "health" block (verified null), so the DEFAULTS above are what actually run.

Partial mitigation, which is why this is bounded rather than total: `new_stuck` (threshold 15000) does catch the decoder-dead variant, because unresolved articles pile up at status 'new' — at ~146 districts x ~4 queries x 15 items it would trip within days. But it does not catch the RSS-blocked/429 variant at all, because then nothing is inserted and every counter simply stops moving. No check anywhere alerts on "counts stopped growing."

Scenario plausibility: high. googlenewsdecoder depends on Google's batchexecute internals and breaks on format changes; GH runner IPs are commonly rate-limited by Google News. The repo's own history (comments citing the 11-14 Jul publish freeze and the 18/20 Jul disk-full outages) shows this class of silent stall has already happened twice.

Severity high is right: the failure is silent, the site actively asserts freshness it does not have, and the one watchdog aimed at it is both unimplemented and, in its shipped form, inverted.

findings.title: Suffixed geocode_method values violate the DB CHECK constraint and wedge the entire geocode stage
findings.evidence: migrations/001_schema.sql:46-48 constrains geocode_method to exactly ('coords_in_text','landmark_district','road_city','city_centroid','district_centroid','manual'); no later migration (002-011) relaxes it. pipeline/processing/geocode.py:228-237 (added in the 2026-07-18 guard-audit) now writes 'landmark_district_unanchored', 'road_city_stateless_hit', '..._wide_area' etc. pipeline/run.py:269-273 and 313-317 UPDATE incident with that value; pipeline/db.py connect() is autocommit=False and cmd_geocode commits only once after the loop (run.py:288). Because the whole batch is one transaction, every geocode in that daily run rolls back; the stage is marked FAILED and, since the poisoned incident still has geom IS NULL, it is re-selected and re-explodes every subsequent run. findings.title: Death-toll follow-up articles are guaranteed to NOT merge, double-counting the same crash's fatalities publicly
findings.evidence: pipeline/processing/dedup.py:27-29: is_same_crash rejects any pair with |Δfatalities| > 1 or |Δinjuries| > 3. Indian crash coverage standardly produces a day-2 'toll rises' follow-up (e.g. 3 dead → 6 dead as injured die in hospital). Both articles pass relevance/extraction independently (store.py near_duplicate won't catch them — different text, Hamming > 3), producing two incidents for one crash whose casualty delta exceeds the compatibility window by construction. cluster.py then puts both in the same hotspot and sums fatalities (cluster.py:49-57, score.py:77); export_public.py publishes hotspot fatality totals and meta.json national totals.
findings.failure_scenario: Crash kills 3 on day 1 ('3 dead'), follow-up on day 2 reports 'toll rises to 6'. Dedup sees Δfat = 3 > 1 → keeps both incidents. The hotspot now shows 2 incidents / 9 fatalities for a single 6-death crash; the 6-month frequency counter counts 2 crashes toward the ≥3 escalation flag; meta.json's headline fatality total is inflated. A journalist or government official cross-checking the cited source articles immediately sees the double count — precisely the credibility failure the CLAUDE.md principles forbid.
findings.fix: Treat casualty-superset pairs specially: if two incidents share date window + tight spatial window and one casualty vector dominates the other (later published_at, higher toll), flag as 'update_candidate' and merge keeping the LATER toll (or route to review) instead of applying the symmetric |Δ| gate. Comparing narrative/location similarity or shared road_name would keep genuinely distinct large crashes apart.

verdict.reason: Evidence checks out line-for-line. /Users/a39002/Documents/Claude/crashfree-infra-repo/pipeline/processing/dedup.py:27-29 hard-rejects any pair with |Δfatalities| > 1 or |Δinjuries| > 3, and this is deliberate, not accidental — tests/test_core_logic.py:174-176 (`test_casualty_mismatch_never_merges`, f=1 vs f=4) locks the behavior in. Nothing anywhere in the repo handles a rising death toll: grep for "toll"/"follow-up"/fatality-update across the pipeline returns only a keyword-pack entry ("death toll" as a relevance term) and an unrelated toll-plaza watch site. The follow-up's crash_date is the original crash date, so it lands inside the ±1-day window and the same 1000 m spatial window — every gate passes except the casualty gate, which fails by construction precisely when the toll jumps by ≥2. store.py:135 near_duplicate (simhash, hamming ≤3, 7-day window) cannot catch differently-worded day-2 copy, and the URL is different. Downstream the double count is live: cluster.py:47-58 sums `sum(fatalities)` over every geocoded incident with geocode_confidence ≥ 0.5 *regardless of publish status*, so even a follow-up that flunks the infra gate and sits in the review queue still inflates hotspot fatality_count and incident_count; score.py:77-79 counts it toward the 6-month `inc_6mo` frequency feeding the ≥3 escalation flag. auto_review.py's `confirm_publish` path auto-approves without any same-crash check, so the inflated hotspot publishes unattended. Two mild qualifiers on the write-up, neither of which refutes it: a +1 toll bump (3→4) does merge correctly, so the failure is specific to jumps of ≥2 fatalities or ≥4 injuries; and the phrase "guaranteed" holds only for that subset. But at 722-district ingestion scale, multi-fatality crashes where hospitalized victims die over the next day are routine in Indian coverage, so recurrence well inside 6 months is near-certain. The failure is also externally auditable — every incident carries its source URL, so a journalist opening the two cited articles sees one crash counted twice, which is exactly the credibility-over-coverage failure CLAUDE.md principle 1 forbids.

findings.title: Nominatim usage-policy violation risk: cold cache + daily repeated identical queries + 'empty MAPBOX_TOKEN = Nominatim only' mode can get the UA banned, silently freezing all publication
findings.evidence: geocode.py:62-82 respects 1.1 s spacing and sends a contact UA (line 35) — good — but the OSMF Nominatim policy also requires that results be cached and prohibits systematic repeated queries and bulk geocoding. Because `data/` is gitignored, every cloud run re-issues identical queries for the same stuck incidents day after day (rescue pass, run.py:296-331). daily.yml:65 explicitly documents the degraded mode: 'MAPBOX_TOKEN ... empty = Nominatim only' — i.e. if the secret is missing/rotated, a 146-district national pipeline runs entirely on the free community Nominatim instance. Residual gap: the 1 req/s limiter is per-process memory (geocode.py:40, `_last_call`), so a manual local run (scripts/daily.sh) or a laptop debugging session running concurrently with the cloud run doubles the aggregate rate under the same identifying UA/email.
findings.failure_scenario: OSM ops sees the same contact-UA issuing the same query set daily at sustained 1 req/s and blocks the UA (their documented enforcement). From then on _nominatim gets non-200s, returns None, and — because there is no alerting on unresolved-rate — every new incident lands ungeocoded or at centroid confidence, fails the 0.6 publish gate, and the public map silently stops gaining pins while the daily run keeps reporting ok=True. Exactly the failure class of the July map freeze, but permanent.
findings.fix: Make the cache persistent (same fix as the Mapbox finding — one DB table solves both policy compliance and quota). Treat Mapbox as mandatory in production: fail the workflow loudly (or Slack-alert) if MAPBOX_TOKEN is empty rather than silently falling back to Nominatim-only. Add a per-run Nominatim call budget (e.g. 500) and an alert when the unresolved/centroid share of the day's geocodes spikes above baseline.

verdict.reason: Core evidence verified: data/ is gitignored and daily.yml has no cache/artifact step, so every cloud run starts with a cold geocode cache and re-issues identical Nominatim queries daily for stuck incidents (run.py:263 geom-is-null pass and 296-331 rescue pass, limit 1000 each; local cache shows 118/161 Nominatim entries are cached misses that would repeat forever in CI). This violates the OSMF caching requirement and matches their documented faulty-client block trigger; the per-process rate limiter and Nominatim-only degraded mode (daily.yml:65) are also real. However, the claimed impact is overstated: (1) health.py's publishing_alive check (built from the July freeze) fires a Slack alert on 0 auto-published at real spend, so a full publication freeze would not be silent or permanent; (2) in normal production Mapbox is primary and the rescue pass is Mapbox-gated, so a Nominatim ban alone only degrades the fallback — catastrophe requires Mapbox loss AND a ban simultaneously; (3) observed Nominatim volume is tens of compliant-rate queries per day with a contact UA, making an outright 6-month ban plausible but not likely. Real compliance gap deserving a fix (persist the cache via actions/cache or stop daily retries of known misses), but medium, not high.

findings.title: Daily job is converging on the GitHub Actions 6-hour hard kill: 330-min timeout, collect alone ~2h at 3 states, and the Nominatim-fallback rescue pass adds up to ~2h more — a timeout also skips the Vercel deploy
findings.evidence: daily.yml:16 `timeout-minutes: 330` with the comment '3 states (BR+UP+RJ, 146 districts) — collect alone can take ~2h'. Adding a state is a config-only change (config_settings.json:57 daily_states). The rescue pass (run.py:296-331) can touch 1000 items x up to 6 variants, and whenever Mapbox misses (typical for exactly the hard-to-geocode stuck items) each variant costs 1.1 s of Nominatim wait (geocode.py:68-71) — several hundred stuck items alone can add 1-2 h. The Vercel deploy step's `!cancelled()` guard (daily.yml:74) does NOT survive a job-level timeout: when timeout-minutes kills the job, remaining steps are cancelled, so no deploy happens.
findings.failure_scenario: A fourth state is added to daily_states (or the stuck-geocode queue grows past a few hundred), the run crosses 330 min, GitHub kills the job mid-stage. pipeline_run is never closed (finished_at stays null), the site is not redeployed, and the 15:00 IST retry re-runs the identical 5.5h+ workload with a cold cache and dies the same way — a permanent every-day double-timeout loop that burns nothing visible except a red X nobody is watching for.
findings.fix: Cut runtime structurally: persist the geocode cache (removes most Nominatim sleeps), cap the rescue batch (e.g. --limit 200/day), and split collect into a per-state matrix of parallel jobs (each state well under 2h). Also bump timeout-minutes only after splitting — 360 is the hard per-job ceiling, so splitting is the real fix — and alert on cancelled/timed-out conclusions, not just failures.

verdict.reason: All evidence verified in-repo: daily.yml:16 has timeout-minutes 330 with the "collect alone ~2h" comment (GitHub hard cap 360); cmd_daily reads config-only daily_states (config_settings.json:57) and calls geocode with limit=1000; the rescue pass (run.py:296-331) falls back to Nominatim per variant despite its "Mapbox only" comment, paying 1.1s spacing (geocode.py:68-71) plus HTTP latency per uncached miss; data/ is gitignored and the workflow has no actions/cache, so the geocode cache is cold every run and the stuck-queue cost repeats daily; job timeout cancels the job so the !cancelled() deploy step (daily.yml:74) is skipped, defeating the run-#9 "always deploy" design; pipeline_run finished_at is only set at the end (run.py:466-470) with no try/finally; the retry guard checks status=success only, so a cancelled run triggers a full re-run. No wall-clock guard, duration alert, or cache persistence exists anywhere — health.py monitors DB/queue/publishing but not runtime, and it runs (with Slack alerting) inside the same job after geocode, so a timeout silences it too. Minor overstatements only: the retry is somewhat lighter than "identical" (processed articles persist in DB, spend baseline carries over), so loop permanence is plausible-borderline rather than certain — but the dominant fixed costs (collect RSS matrix, cold-cache geocode) do repeat in full.

findings.title: GitHub auto-disables the cron after 60 days without repo activity — the pipeline writes only to Supabase, never commits, so once development stops the whole cloud pipeline silently dies
findings.evidence: daily.yml:3-7 — the entire production pipeline hangs off `on: schedule` in a public repo (README: 'runs fully in the cloud ... public repo = unlimited free minutes'). GitHub's documented behavior: scheduled workflows are disabled automatically after 60 days of repository inactivity (no commits), with a single warning email. Nothing in the daily run pushes a commit — all writes go to Supabase and Vercel — so repo activity is purely development churn.
findings.failure_scenario: The project reaches steady state (it is already 'FULLY CLOUD-AUTONOMOUS'), commits stop for two months, GitHub disables daily.yml. Both crons stop; no run failure ever fires because no run happens; the dashboard just quietly stops updating. Given the self-healing-retry design assumes failures produce red runs, a disabled schedule is the one outage mode the current alerting cannot see.
findings.fix: Two independent guards: 1) a tiny monthly keepalive workflow that pushes an empty commit or calls `gh api repos/.../actions/workflows/daily.yml/enable`; 2) an external freshness monitor on the already-exported `meta.json` `generated_at` field (export_public.py:94) — e.g. a scheduled check elsewhere (or an uptime service) that alerts Slack when generated_at is older than 36h. The second guard also catches every other silent-death mode in this list.

verdict.reason: Verified: daily.yml:3-7 triggers only on schedule/workflow_dispatch in a public repo (README:250-251 confirms 'fully in the cloud', 'public repo = unlimited free minutes'); no workflow step commits or pushes (all writes go to Supabase and Vercel); no keepalive, external heartbeat, or uptime monitor exists anywhere in the repo; Slack alerting (pipeline/processing/health.py, watch.py) runs inside the pipeline so a never-started run emits zero signal. GitHub's 60-day inactivity auto-disable of scheduled workflows in public repos is documented behavior, and scheduled runs do not count as activity. The repo went fully autonomous 2026-07-04 with no-commits steady state as the design goal, so 60 commit-free days within 6 months is the expected trajectory. Aggravating detail: the run uses --days 2 collection lookback (daily.yml:68), so the outage window's data cannot be backfilled after re-enabling — silent outage plus unrecoverable data gap.

findings.title: Google News RSS + redirector decoding has zero 429 handling and fails silently — the sole primary ingestion source can be throttled to nothing (shared GH-runner IPs) while the run reports ok=True; unresolved articles are stored as 'new' and never retried
findings.evidence: rss.py:108-110: `r.raise_for_status()` with no 429 backoff (contrast gdelt.py:51-59, which does back off). run.py:44-47 catches the exception, increments stats['errors'] and continues — the collect stage still 'succeeds'. Per run: ~146 districts x up to 4 queries = ~580 RSS hits to news.google.com from shared GitHub-runner IPs, plus one googlenewsdecoder batchexecute round-trip per article (rss.py:96-99) — Google's classic throttle points. When the decoder is throttled, resolved=False, and run.py:60 (`if not args.no_fetch and it.resolved`) skips the body fetch, storing the row with processing_status='new' (run.py:57) — and no code path anywhere reprocesses status 'new' (cmd_process reads only 'fetched', run.py:143), so those articles are permanently lost.
findings.failure_scenario: Google rate-limits the runner IP block for a day (or tightens redirector decoding, which has broken this library repeatedly): the day's collection collapses to near-zero or to unresolved 'new' rows that are never fetched. All stages report success, ok=True, the site redeploys with stale data, and days of vernacular evidence — the core asset — are unrecoverable because the `when:2d` recency window has moved on by the time anyone notices.
findings.fix: 1) Handle 429/redirect-loop from news.google.com with exponential backoff + jitter, mirroring the GDELT collector. 2) Add a canary check at the end of collect: if stored-new articles < ~25% of the trailing-7-day median, mark the run degraded and Slack-alert. 3) Add a retry sweep that re-attempts resolve+fetch for status='new' rows from the last 3 days at the start of each daily run. 4) If throttling recurs, route resolution through Apify (already in the team's toolbox) or a self-hosted runner with a stable IP.

verdict.reason: Every evidence claim verified against the code: rss.py:108-110 has raise_for_status() with no 429 backoff (gdelt.py:51-59 does back off); run.py:44-47 swallows RSS exceptions into stats['errors'] so collect 'succeeds' and ok=True; unresolved articles are stored processing_status='new' (run.py:57) with fetch skipped (run.py:58), and no code path anywhere reprocesses 'new' (cmd_process reads only 'fetched', run.py:143) — the rss.py docstring even promises a retry that was never built. District math is exact: 146 districts (BR+UP+RJ per config_settings.json daily_states), ~580 RSS hits/run from ubuntu-latest shared runner IPs. The finding actually understates it: GDELT is not part of the daily run (cmd_daily passes gdelt=None) so RSS is the sole production source; the 15:00 IST self-healing retry only fires on workflow failure, which silent 429 swallowing prevents; and health.py is blind to collapse (publishing_alive passes when spend < $0.10, new_stuck alerts only at 15,000, and min_extracted_last_run is defined but never checked). Scenario is realistic within 6 months at current volume. Medium is the right severity: loss is bounded by ~1 day of when:2d window overlap and chronic pileup eventually trips new_stuck_alert.

findings.title: Nightly recompute rewrites every geocoded incident and every hotspot row (twice) in single transactions — O(N) WAL/dead-tuple churn that grows forever; incident/hotspot are never vacuumed
findings.evidence: cluster.py:27-34 runs ST_ClusterDBSCAN over ALL geocoded incidents with no date horizon, minpoints := 1 (config cluster_min_points=1), so every incident belongs to a cluster and cluster count grows ~linearly with incidents. cluster.py:92 `update incident set cluster_id=%s where id = any(%s)` executes for every cluster — every geocoded incident row is rewritten nightly even when cluster_id is unchanged. cluster.py:75-81 updates every matched hotspot unconditionally (last_recomputed_at=now() forces a rewrite). score.py:107-111 then updates every hotspot AGAIN with a ~1-2KB score_breakdown jsonb. All inside one commit each (cluster.py:93, score.py:112). The hygiene stage vacuums ONLY source_article (run.py:456); incident, hotspot, review_action rely on autovacuum, which the nightly long transactions hold back. The per-cluster loop also issues ~5 round-trip queries per cluster (cluster.py:48-92) and score.py ~3 per hotspot — O(N) pooler round-trips nightly.
findings.failure_scenario: At ~20-40 incidents/day, after 12 months there are ~10k geocoded incidents and (with minpoints=1) thousands of hotspots: nightly churn = ~10k incident row rewrites + 2× hotspot rewrites + jsonb payloads → tens of MB of WAL and an equal count of dead tuples EVERY night on a Supabase instance that already had a disk-full outage from write amplification (18 Jul). Bloat on incident/hotspot compounds because nothing vacuums them and the nightly full-table update keeps re-creating dead tuples. Runtime grows too: ~5 round-trips × N clusters over the session pooler ≈ 30-70 min at 10k clusters, on top of geocode/collect growth — combined 330-min timeout breach in the 6-12 month range, and disk-pressure incidents before that.
findings.fix: (1) Skip no-op writes: `update incident set cluster_id=%s where id=any(%s) and cluster_id is distinct from %s`, and only update hotspot rows whose aggregate values actually changed. (2) Add a clustering horizon (e.g. incidents with crash_date/created_at in the last 24 months) or recluster only districts touched since the last run. (3) Set minpoints=2 or defer hotspot-row creation until a cluster has ≥2 incidents so hotspot count stops tracking incident count 1:1. (4) Batch the per-cluster queries (execute_values / one aggregate query grouped by cl). (5) Extend the hygiene vacuum to incident, hotspot, review_action.

verdict.reason: Every code citation checks out: cluster.py:33 hardcodes minpoints:=1 with no date horizon (config cluster_min_points=1), cluster.py:92 rewrites cluster_id on every geocoded incident nightly, hotspots are rewritten twice (cluster.py:75-81, score.py:107-111 with jsonb), ~5 round-trips/cluster + 3/hotspot over the session pooler, and run.py:456 vacuums only source_article. Empirical confirmation in bihar_run.log: 52 incidents produced 45 hotspots, so hotspot count really tracks incident count linearly. However the severity is overstated on two axes: (1) Supabase autovacuum does reclaim incident/hotspot dead tuples between nightly runs, so the claimed compounding bloat / disk-pressure incidents don't materialize — steady-state bloat is bounded and the tables are small (no raw_html-scale payloads; WAL is single-digit-to-tens of MB nightly and recycled, unlike the 1.5GB 18-Jul mechanism); (2) growth is throttled by the $0.98/day extraction budget (~15-35 geocoded incidents/day), so at 6 months (~2.5-5k hotspots) the added recompute wall-time is roughly 20-80 min against a 330-min budget — real linear runtime degradation, but timeout breach lands at 12+ months, not 6. Genuine unbounded-growth defect worth fixing (add a horizon or dirty-only updates, raise min_points, batch queries), but medium not high.

findings.title: clean_text is kept forever for every article including irrelevant/near_duplicate/failed — the next raw_html-style hoard, ~2-5 MB/day toward the 400 MB alert
findings.evidence: Hygiene (run.py:449-451) nulls ONLY raw_html on terminal articles; clean_text is inserted for every fetched article (run.py:76, watch.py:77) and never pruned anywhere. Consumers of clean_text are all time-bounded: watch name-matching looks back 3 days (watch.py:93-95, LOOKBACK_DAYS=3), auto_review reads it only while an incident is verification_status='auto' (auto_review.py:117-124), processing reads only status='fetched'. clean_text on irrelevant/near_duplicate/failed articles older than a few days serves zero code paths. Calibration: raw_html reached 1.5GB in ~2 weeks (run.py:445-447 comment), i.e. ~100MB/day of pages; at a typical 20-50:1 html:text ratio clean_text accrues ~2-5MB/day.
findings.failure_scenario: At ~2-5MB/day, clean_text alone adds ~60-150MB per month. Combined with review_action and table bloat, the health db_size alert (400MB, health.py:18) trips in roughly 3-8 months, and the Supabase free 500MB hard limit — the exact cause of the 18 Jul outage — follows weeks later. Unlike raw_html there is then no obvious one-line purge because the terminal-status rows are the majority of the table.
findings.fix: Extend the hygiene UPDATE: null clean_text (optionally keeping `left(clean_text, 500)` as an evidence stub) on articles in ('irrelevant','near_duplicate','failed') older than 7 days, and on 'extracted' articles whose incidents have left 'auto' status (verification_status not in ('auto')) older than 30 days — evidence_snippet rows in incident_defect already preserve the quoted proof. Keep dedup_hash and url so dedup semantics are untouched.

verdict.reason: Verified in code: hygiene (run.py:450-451) nulls only raw_html; clean_text is inserted for every fetched article (run.py:75-77, watch.py:76-78) and no code path anywhere prunes it. Standing consumers are all time-bounded exactly as claimed (watch 3-day lookback, auto_review only while verification_status='auto', processing only status='fetched'); only ad-hoc repair scripts ever touch older clean_text. Measured production DB read-only: clean_text totals 28 MB after ~2 weeks, 68% of it on terminal rows (near_duplicate 15.9 MB, irrelevant 3.1 MB); steady-state accrual ~1.2-3.6 MB/day (mean ~1.7, slightly below the claimed 2-5), whole source_article table growing ~3.2 MB/day. From today's 68 MB DB, the 400 MB health alert trips in ~3.5-4 months and the Supabase 500 MB hard limit ~1 month later — within the claimed window and within 6 months. The health watchdog only warns; nothing remediates.

findings.title: near_duplicate check runs an unindexed scan of the whole source_article table per fetched article — O(total table size) per insert, table grows forever
findings.evidence: store.py:146-155 filters on `dedup_hash is not null and dedup_hash != '' and fetched_at > now() - make_interval(...) and district = %s`, then pulls ALL matching hashes into Python and computes Hamming distance per hash (fetch.py:96-105). 001_schema.sql:26-28 defines indexes only on processing_status, dedup_hash, and published_at — there is no index on fetched_at or district, so the planner has no selective path and seq-scans the heap for every candidate article during collect (~300-800 calls/day at current fetch volume, one per non-dup-URL item, run.py:64-66; watch.py:70 adds more).
findings.failure_scenario: The scanned table grows without bound (findings #4 and #5 guarantee it: dead 'new' rows, terminal rows never deleted). At ~400 rows/day the table passes 100k+ rows within a year; several hundred seq scans/day over an ever-larger heap add steadily growing minutes to the collect stage (already ~2h per daily.yml:16) and steady read I/O against Supabase. Degradation is gradual then compounds with every other growth finding toward the 330-min timeout.
findings.fix: Add a partial composite index: `create index if not exists idx_source_article_dedup_scope on source_article (district, fetched_at) where dedup_hash is not null and dedup_hash <> '';` (state variant likewise or include state as a column). Query cost drops from O(table) to O(recent district rows). Optionally also cap the fetched set with `limit 2000` as a safety valve.

verdict.reason: All evidence verified against the code. store.py:135-155 DBStore.near_duplicate filters on dedup_hash-not-null/non-empty, a 7-day fetched_at window, and district (state fallback), then pulls all matching hashes into Python and computes per-hash Hamming distance via fetch.py:96-105. Migrations 001-011 define indexes only on processing_status, dedup_hash, and published_at — no index on fetched_at or district, and the dedup_hash index is useless here since its only predicate (is not null / != '') matches nearly every row, so each call is a full heap scan. Call sites confirmed: run.py:64-66 invokes it once per fetched non-duplicate-URL item across 146 districts in 3 states (daily.yml:16, collect ~2h, 330-min timeout), plus watch.py:70 — several hundred calls/day is realistic. No delete on source_article exists anywhere; the hygiene stage only nulls raw_html and vacuums, so the scanned table grows without bound. Severity check: per-scan cost at 6 months (~50-75k rows, raw_html purged) is likely sub-second, and collect time is network-dominated, so this alone will not hit the 330-min timeout in 6 months — but it is a genuine O(table)-per-insert pattern on an already disk-constrained Supabase instance, guaranteed to compound with the other growth findings, and trivially fixable with an index on (district, fetched_at). Medium is appropriate.

findings.title: 'fetched' extraction queue can diverge without backpressure — ingestion volume is fixed while processing throughput is budget-capped
findings.evidence: Collect ingests 3 states / 146 districts daily (config daily_states) regardless of queue state; cmd_process stops at the $0.975 extraction share (run.py:159-164, llmcost.over) leaving the remainder as status='fetched' "for tomorrow" — but tomorrow brings the same inflow. health.py:19 alerts at 4000 queued (monitor only, no throttle). The defect-terms priority sort (run.py:147-150) means behaviour-only articles can sit in the queue permanently, holding full clean_text (finding #5) forever.
findings.failure_scenario: If steady-state inflow of extractable articles exceeds ~what $1/day buys (~20-40 sonnet extractions plus haiku relevance calls), the queue grows by the difference daily: the 4000 alert trips in a few months, the oldest queued articles are permanently starved by the priority sort, and their retained clean_text compounds DB growth. Widening beyond 3 states makes divergence near-certain.
findings.fix: Add backpressure or aging: (1) in health.py, when queue_depth alert fires, have cmd_daily reduce collect scope (or raise the budget) rather than only alerting; (2) age out queue members — articles 'fetched' for >30 days flip to 'irrelevant' with a review_action note (they are stale news by then), which also makes them eligible for the clean_text purge; (3) expose queue-age p95 in pipeline_run stage_stats so divergence is visible before the absolute threshold.

verdict.reason: Confirmed in code and empirically in the production DB: fetched queue is at 3158 (79% of the 4000 alert), having grown 0->3158 in the last six days (~+450-500/day) while every run since 7/11 saturated the $1.95 daily LLM cap — ingestion of 146 districts is unconditional (config daily_states), extraction stops at the $0.975 share (run.py:158-164), and health.py:19 only Slack-alerts with no throttle. The finding's mechanism is correct and its timeline understated (alert trips in days, not months). Two claimed details are weaker: the 1000-id-ordered fetch window means the oldest articles are not permanently starved (the unprocessed tail is the newest), and queued clean_text is only 6.2MB against a 68MB DB (400MB alert), so the DB-growth compounding is minor.

findings.title: GitHub fine-grained PAT embedded in the git remote URL (and .env) — expires within a year, two copies to rotate, config-drift cascade when it dies
findings.evidence: `git config remote.origin.url` = https://DeepanshuCFI:***@github.com/DeepanshuCFI/cfi-defect-repository.git, and the same token sits in .env as GITHUB_TOKEN. Grep shows NO code reads GITHUB_TOKEN, and CI uses the ephemeral `github.token` (daily.yml guard step) — the PAT's only real job is local push/pull, yet it lives in two places. credential.helper=osxkeychain is configured but never consulted because URL-embedded credentials take precedence. Repo history begins ~2026-07-04: a 90-day default PAT expires ~early Oct 2026; even the 1-year max dies by Jul 2027.
findings.failure_scenario: PAT expires → local `git push`/`git pull` returns 401. The dangerous part is the cascade: GitHub Actions is the sole production runner and daily.yml's 'Sync configs to DB (git config/ is the source of truth)' step reloads config from git every morning. An operator who cannot push and instead patches config directly in the DB (scripts/load_configs.py locally) gets silently reverted by the next CI run — production config rolls back every night with no signal. Meanwhile the expired token remains in the remote URL, so fixing keychain auth alone does nothing.
findings.fix: Run `git remote set-url origin https://github.com/DeepanshuCFI/cfi-defect-repository.git` and let osxkeychain/gh CLI supply auth (or switch to an SSH deploy key, which never expires); delete the unused GITHUB_TOKEN line from .env. When minting the replacement PAT, record its expiry. Add a probe to check-secrets: GET https://api.github.com/user with the PAT and read the `github-authentication-token-expiration` response header; fail the workflow when <14 days remain.

verdict.reason: All evidence verified: fine-grained PAT is embedded verbatim in remote.origin.url and duplicated in .env (line 8); grep confirms no code reads GITHUB_TOKEN; daily.yml uses ephemeral github.token (line 23) and its config-sync step (lines 52-56) re-upserts config/ from git twice daily, so un-pushed DB-side config edits genuinely revert silently; osxkeychain helper is set but URL-embedded creds take precedence; repo starts 2026-07-04 so a default-lifetime fine-grained PAT expires within ~6 months. Token works today (git ls-remote succeeded). However, severity high overstates blast radius: CI/production is fully decoupled from the PAT, the primary failure is a loud 401 on local push with a minutes-long fix, and the dangerous silent-revert cascade only fires if the operator works around auth failure by patching the DB instead of rotating the token — a plausible but conditional second-order path. Real finding, medium severity.

findings.title: DATABASE_URL: one DB password in three unsynchronized stores, on a Pro-migration-sensitive pooler hostname
findings.evidence: .env has DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres.lzybxtfrlsphtqfxidyn:***@aws-0-ap-northeast-1.pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres; the identical value must also live in GitHub Actions secrets (daily.yml) and Render env (render.yaml, sync:false). health.py's comment ('free limit was 500; Pro is 8GB') confirms the recent free→Pro upgrade. review/app.py:92-96 documents that Render already 500s on stale pooled connections after sleep — the same symptom a dead credential would produce.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) Someone resets the DB password in the Supabase dashboard (routine during a leak scare or the Pro migration): all three consumers die at once. CI fails loudly at the unguarded 'Sync configs to DB' step (red run + email), but the Render review console just starts 500ing on the next reviewer visit — indistinguishable from the known pooler-sleep 500s, so it gets misdiagnosed for days while the queue is unworkable. (b) Supabase changes the shared pooler endpoint (aws-0 → aws-1 renumbering has happened for other projects; Pro's dedicated pooler / IPv4 add-on uses a different hostname): failure presents as DNS/connection-refused, not auth, in all three places simultaneously.
findings.fix: Write a 3-line rotation checklist in the README ops section naming all three copy locations (local .env, GitHub Actions secret, Render env). After the Pro upgrade, diff the dashboard's current pooler connection string against the stored one today. Add a `select 1` connectivity probe against the DATABASE_URL secret to the monthly check-secrets job. Ideally give Render its own DB role/password so review-console credentials rotate independently and its failures are distinguishable.

verdict.reason: All five evidence points verified in the repo: .env holds the pooler DATABASE_URL (store 1), daily.yml consumes secrets.DATABASE_URL (store 2), render.yaml declares it sync:false for manual Render-dashboard entry (store 3), health.py's 'free limit was 500; Pro is 8GB' comment confirms the recent Pro migration, and review/app.py:92-96 documents real prior 500s (reject #1102) from stale pooled connections — the same symptom a rotated password would produce. No rotation runbook exists, and check-secrets.yml validates only secret presence, not validity, so nothing detects a dead credential in the Render copy. A Supabase password reset within 6 months is routine ops (and this .env's plaintext live secrets make a leak-scare rotation especially plausible), so the three-store desync scenario is realistic. Minor nits (the sync step is if-guarded for skip logic, and the retry wrapper now mitigates pure sleep-500s) don't undermine the core finding.

findings.title: check-secrets workflow proves PRESENCE, never VALIDITY — every expiry in this audit passes it green
findings.evidence: check-secrets.yml only tests `[ -n "$v" ]` per secret (its own comment says 'presence only'), and it is workflow_dispatch-only — it never runs unless a human remembers to click it. It also reports SUPABASE_URL/SUPABASE_KEY, which no code consumes (see finding 9), manufacturing false comfort.
findings.failure_scenario: An expired PAT, Vercel token, Anthropic key, Mapbox token, or rotated DB password all report PRESENT forever. The one ops tool built for secret hygiene actively reassures the team while credentials are dead.
findings.fix: Add a `validate` job on `schedule: cron '0 3 1 * *'` (monthly) plus dispatch, with cheap read-only probes: psql `select 1` for DATABASE_URL; GET api.anthropic.com/v1/models for ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; `npx vercel whoami --token $VERCEL_TOKEN`; GET api.mapbox.com/search/geocode/v6/forward?q=Delhi&access_token=... expecting 200; GET api.github.com/user with the PAT (plus its expiration header); and POST a one-line 'monthly credential probe OK' to SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL — the 2xx doubles as the webhook's own probe. Any failure exits non-zero, so a GitHub failure email fires through a channel independent of Slack.

verdict.reason: Evidence verified: check-secrets.yml tests only [ -n "$v" ] (self-labeled "presence only"), is workflow_dispatch-only, and reports SUPABASE_URL/SUPABASE_KEY which no code consumes (loaded in pipeline/settings.py lines 13-14, referenced nowhere else). The silent-expiry scenario is real for three secrets: a dead ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is WARN'd through per-article in run.py cmd_process so the workflow stays green while publishing nothing (this exact channel caused the documented 13 Jul incident of 424 articles WARN'd through, and the 11-14 Jul map freeze); an expired MAPBOX_TOKEN silently falls back to Nominatim (geocode.py line 104); a revoked SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL is a printed WARN only and is the delivery channel for all other alerts. health.py even defines min_extracted_last_run ("0 extractions = API silently dead") but never implements the check, and publishing_alive passes at zero spend. Two corrections that cap severity: DATABASE_URL and VERCEL_TOKEN failures fail the twice-daily workflow loudly within 24h (de facto validity checks), and no PAT is among the checked secrets (daily.yml uses ephemeral github.token), so the scenario's PAT mention is wrong. Core finding stands: zero validity monitoring anywhere, and the presence-only tool is green precisely for the credentials that die silently.

findings.title: Invalid (vs absent) MAPBOX_TOKEN silently degrades geocoding quality and poisons the local cache
findings.evidence: geocode.py:100-117 — non-200 from Mapbox yields feats=[] → result None, and a bare `except Exception` also yields None; _resolve() then falls back to Nominatim, which the module docstring itself calls far weaker on Indic village/tehsil text. Line 118 caches the None (`cache[key] = result`) even for provider errors, permanently negative-caching those queries in data/geocode_cache.json locally. run.py:295 gates the Mapbox rescue pass on token PRESENCE (`if MAPBOX_TOKEN:`), not validity — so an invalid token still runs the rescue loop and rescues nothing.
findings.failure_scenario: The default public token is rotated/deleted in the Mapbox dashboard, the account downgrades, or the free 100k/month geocoding quota is exhausted mid-month → every call 401/429s. No stage fails, the run stays green; geocode_confidence quietly sags, fewer incidents cross the 0.6 publish bar, the geocode-blocked queue stops melting. The only trace is a shifted 'Geocode confidence by method' table on /qa that nobody is watching for this. Locally, the poisoned negative cache keeps returning Nominatim-grade answers even after the token is fixed.
findings.fix: In _mapbox, distinguish provider errors from genuine no-result: do not cache on non-200/exception, and after N consecutive failures surface a 'mapbox_dead' flag into the stage stats and a health.py check. Add the Mapbox 200-probe to the monthly check-secrets job.

verdict.reason: All cited evidence verified in code: geocode.py:104 treats non-200 (401/429) as feats=[] and line 116's bare except yields None, both indistinguishable from a genuine miss; line 118 negative-caches provider-error Nones under the mb| key and lines 91-93 return that cached None permanently (local cache only — data/ is gitignored and daily.yml does a fresh checkout, so cloud runs don't persist the poison). run.py:295 gates the rescue pass on token presence, not validity, so an invalid token runs a rescue loop that can rescue nothing. No token validation, error counting, or alerting exists anywhere (only settings.py:16, geocode.py, run.py:295 reference MAPBOX); cmd_daily stages only fail on exceptions, which _mapbox swallows, so the run stays green while geocode_confidence sags below the 0.6 publish gate (CLAUDE.md) and the only trace is the passive 'Geocode confidence by method' table at review/app.py:175. Trigger plausibility within 6 months is solid: token rotation is routine, and because cloud runs have no persistent cache, each daily run re-issues Mapbox queries for the whole rescue queue (up to 1000 items × several ladder variants), making mid-month quota exhaustion realistic. Severity stays medium because the degradation is fail-closed for credibility — nothing wrong publishes, items pile into review — so it's silent throughput loss, not data corruption.

findings.title: SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL is the single alert channel, and its own death is silent
findings.evidence: watch.py:149-156 — non-2xx from the webhook → `print WARN`, return {sent: 0}, stage still succeeds and ok stays True. health.py run() wraps its alert POST in `except Exception → print WARN` — the alert is simply lost. Both site-watch pings AND every health-watchdog alert (db size, queue depth, publishing_alive — the only backstops for findings 1 and 6) ride this one webhook.
findings.failure_scenario: The Slack app is removed, the channel is archived, or the webhook is regenerated during a workspace cleanup. From that day: site-watch hits and all health alerts vanish; runs remain green; 'no news' reads as 'all good'. Because the webhook is also the delivery path for the queue_depth alarm, a dead Anthropic key (finding 1) plus a dead webhook is a compound silent failure with no bounded discovery time.
findings.fix: Treat alert-delivery failure as a health failure: on non-2xx, record 'alerting_dead' in pipeline_run stage stats and flip ok=False (making GitHub email the fallback channel). Include the webhook POST probe in the monthly check-secrets job, whose failure notifies via GitHub — an alert path independent of Slack.

verdict.reason: Verified in code: watch.py:149-156 swallows non-2xx webhook responses (print WARN, sent:0, stage succeeds, ok stays True per run.py:396-405). health.py is worse than claimed — its POST (lines 76-79) never checks r.status_code and httpx does not raise on HTTP errors, so a revoked webhook (Slack returns 404) is dropped with no WARN at all, and health alerts have no persistence or retry unlike watch hits. Grep confirms SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL is the sole alert channel repo-wide; check-secrets.yml is manual and presence-only (a regenerated webhook still reads PRESENT); GitHub failure emails never fire because a dead webhook never fails the run. The four health checks including publishing_alive and queue_depth all ride this one webhook, so the compound silent-failure scenario with a dead Anthropic key is structurally accurate. Minor mitigation: watch hits stay notified=false and surface on the review console, but health alerts vanish entirely.

findings.title: cmd_process limit=1000 with ORDER BY id: the defect-first prioritisation is applied AFTER the limit, so once the backlog exceeded 1,000 (16 Jul) fresh defect stories can no longer jump the queue — and 1,000/day becomes the hard ceiling the moment the budget is raised
findings.evidence: store.py:78-86: articles_by_status runs 'order by id limit %s' — oldest 1,000 only. run.py:143-150 then sorts those 1,000 by defect vocabulary ('budget goes to the mission-critical class first'). cmd_daily passes limit=1000 (run.py:440). Queue is 3,158 today, so the 2,158 newest articles — including every defect story collected in the last ~5 days — are not even candidates for the sort.
findings.failure_scenario: Since ~16 Jul the stated owner policy (defect-vocabulary stories processed before behaviour-only crashes) silently operates only within the oldest-1,000 window: a pothole-collapse story collected today waits ~6+ days (and growing) behind FIFO backlog before it can even be considered. Separately, if the budget is ever raised to clear the backlog, limit=1000 becomes the new binding cap (national inflow ~2,100-3,200 fetched/day > 1,000), and the same divergence resumes with no budget message in the logs — the run reports success.
findings.fix: Move the priority into SQL: ORDER BY (clean_text ~ defect-term regex) DESC, id ASC in articles_by_status (or a two-pass fetch: defect-matching rows first, then FIFO remainder), and raise/remove the limit since the budget already bounds spend — the limit only bounds fairness.

verdict.reason: All evidence verified: store.py:78-86 fetches oldest-1000 by id before run.py:143-150 applies the defect-first sort (limit=1000 at run.py:440). Live DB confirms fetched backlog is exactly 3,158, crossed 1,000 on 16 Jul (cumulative 79/508/881/1,303 by date), and pipeline_run telemetry shows daily spend at $1.90-1.96 of the $2 cap with process reporting 'done' — budget-bound every day while backlog grows, so the 2,158 newest articles (including all defect stories since ~16 Jul) never enter the prioritisation sort. Nothing else drains the fetched queue (watch.py only adds to it). The divergence from the stated owner policy is active now, not hypothetical, and invisible in run status.

findings.title: auto_review limit=200/day is a hard-coded ceiling ~2.4x above current adjudication volume; at national scale with a raised budget the 'auto' queue diverges and publication silently stalls
findings.evidence: auto_review.py:109 'def run(limit: int = 200)' and cmd_daily calls stage('auto_review', ar.run) with no argument (run.py:443) — the 200 is not in config. Measured adjudication rate: 79-83 reviewed/day (runs 16-17 stage_stats), currently capped by the shared $1.95 budget (~$0.011/adjudication on sonnet ≈ 90/day max), with the 'auto' queue at 0 — it keeps up today only because extraction is equally budget-starved.
findings.failure_scenario: Adjudication gates publication (only auto_review flips incidents to auto_published). At 722 districts with the budget raised to converge extraction (~300-450 incidents/day needing adjudication), limit=200 binds: 100-250 incidents/day accumulate in verification_status='auto', FIFO 'order by r.id limit 200' means new incidents wait weeks, and the run reports reviewed=200 as success — no error anywhere. Repeat of the 11-14 Jul map freeze in a new costume.
findings.fix: Move the limit to config (processing.auto_review_daily_limit), pass it from cmd_daily, and size it to incident inflow; the budget already provides the real safety cap. Add left-in-queue count to stage_stats so divergence is visible.

verdict.reason: All evidence verified: limit=200 hard-coded in auto_review.py:109, called with no arg at run.py:443, absent from config (violating the repo's own config-not-code rule); budget $1.95/day in config is today's binding constraint, so the limit binds exactly when the budget is raised for scale. The health watchdog monitors the extraction queue and publishing_alive only — neither detects an adjudication ('auto') backlog, and reviewed=200 reports as success, so divergence is silent. One overstatement: publication doesn't stall, it continues at 200/day while new incidents queue behind a growing FIFO backlog — practically the same freeze for fresh incidents. Plausible within 6 months given the stated national-scale goal.
