findings.title: Web frontend loads every public incident as one incidents.json and runs an O(hotspots x incidents) scan per filter change — usable to ~5-10k incidents, dead well before national volumes; Vercel's 100 MB per-file deploy limit lands at ~50k incidents
findings.evidence: App.jsx:29-33 fetches all of hotspots.geojson + incidents.json up front; App.jsx:65-68 (road filter) executes data.inc.filter(i => i.hotspot_id === p.id) inside the per-hotspot filter loop — O(H x I) on every filter interaction. Measured payload: 430 public incidents = ~850 KB (~2 KB/incident, incidents.json embeds defects + all sources per incident). Publication rate ~55-70/day at the current budget.
findings.failure_scenario: Timeline at current publish rate: ~10k incidents (~20 MB JSON, ~4 MB gzip) in ~5 months — multi-second parse on mobile and visible jank; ~24k (~1 year) — 100M+ comparisons per road-filter change with a few thousand hotspots, multi-second main-thread freezes; ~50k incidents — incidents.json crosses Vercel's documented 100 MB per-deployment-file limit and the deploy step itself starts failing (site stops updating). At national scale with a converged budget (~300+ published/day) these thresholds arrive 5x faster: unusable inside ~2 months.
findings.fix: Split the export: keep hotspots.geojson slim for the map, shard incidents per hotspot (data/incidents/{hotspot_id}.json, fetched lazily when the Drawer opens), and precompute hotspot_id -> road_types into hotspot properties so the road filter never touches the incident list. This also removes the single-file Vercel ceiling.

verdict.reason: Code evidence fully verified: App.jsx:29-33 fetches all incidents.json up front (same in the deployed Vercel bundle), and App.jsx:65-68 runs data.inc.filter(i => i.hotspot_id === p.id) inside the per-hotspot filter loop — O(H x I) per road-filter change, with no precomputed road_type on hotspot properties (checked hotspots.geojson), no pagination, and no index anywhere in web/src. Deploy is `npx vercel deploy` from web/, so the 100 MB per-file limit applies to the append-only incidents.json. Minor overstatements: payload is ~1.6 KB/incident locally (322 KB / 201 incidents), not ~2 KB, and the claimed 55-70/day publish rate could not be confirmed — observed local data suggests ~15-25/day with only 3 of the planned national states collected, pushing the ~10k-incident jank threshold to ~12+ months rather than ~5 at current scope. But the repo's explicit trajectory is national (722-district config), growth is monotonic, and the design has no incremental path — the scaling ceiling is real even if the timeline is ~2x stretched. Side observation: the production /data/*.json endpoints currently return 404, which is worth separate attention.

findings.title: export_public.py issues 2 sequential queries per incident (N+1) over a cross-region pooler connection — export time grows linearly and collides with the workflow timeout at ~10-20k public incidents
findings.evidence: export_public.py:76-91: for every public_incident row, one query for defects and one for sources, sequentially on a single connection (GitHub runner in US, Supabase pooler; ~100-250 ms RTT each). Currently 430 public incidents = ~860 round-trips (~2-4 min). The whole result set is also built in memory before one json.dumps.
findings.failure_scenario: At 10k public incidents: ~20k round-trips ≈ 35-80 min for export alone; at 50k: 2-7 hours — the export stage alone can eat the remaining workflow window after collect, so the deploy that 'always runs' starts being timeout-cancelled precisely when the dataset is most valuable. Memory stays manageable (2 KB/incident) — the round-trips are the killer.
findings.fix: Replace the per-incident loops with three set-based queries using json_agg (defects and sources grouped by incident_id joined in one pass), and stream-write with json.dump. Cuts export to seconds at any realistic scale.

verdict.reason: Confirmed: export_public.py:76-90 issues 2 sequential queries per public_incident on one connection; DATABASE_URL is the Supabase session pooler in ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo) while GitHub runners are US-based, so ~0.1-0.25s per round-trip is realistic. Export runs inside the daily job's 330-min timeout where collect alone already takes ~2h, and a timeout cancels the !cancelled()-gated Vercel deploy, so the 'stale site' failure mode the workflow explicitly guards against returns. Math holds: 10k incidents ≈ 33-83 min, 20k ≈ 66-166 min of pure round-trips. Only soft spot: at current 3-state growth (~25/day, 201→~430 in 9 days) 6 months yields ~5k incidents, below the collision point — reaching 10-20k requires state expansion, which is the locked national roadmap (BUILD_SPEC §3, 722-district config) and compounds the squeeze by also growing collect time. Real, monotonic degradation with an easy batched-query fix; collision likely 3-9 months out.

findings.title: Geocode provider death is silently downgraded: expired Mapbox token degrades everything to Nominatim, failed lookups are cached as misses, and the rescue pass quietly stops rescuing
findings.evidence: geocode.py:100-119 (_mapbox) and 62-82 (_nominatim): any non-200 (e.g. 401 from a rotated token, 429, 5xx) or exception -> result None -> `cache[key] = None` caches the FAILURE as a permanent miss for the rest of the run; geo() itself can never raise, so the geocode stage cannot fail on total provider death. run.py:294-295: if MAPBOX_TOKEN is empty the rescue pass is skipped with only a missing print. run.py:296-331: rescue re-queries up to 1000 stuck items every single day with no retry cap or terminal state (and since data/ is gitignored, the cache file never persists between Actions runs — every lookup is re-paid daily).
findings.failure_scenario: Mapbox token is rotated/expires. All _mapbox calls 401 -> silent fallback to Nominatim (1.1s/lookup, much weaker on Indic village/tehsil text) -> geocode_confidence lands below the 0.6 publish bar far more often -> the geocode-blocked review queue grows instead of melting, publications shrink, and the geocode stage reports 'done' every day. Time to notice: weeks — only via the /qa geocode-method distribution drifting, and only if someone looks.
findings.fix: Count provider outcomes per run (mapbox_ok, mapbox_http_error, nominatim_fallback, unresolved) and return them from cmd_geocode into stage_stats; in cmd_daily flip ok=False when MAPBOX_TOKEN is set but mapbox_ok==0 across >20 attempts (token dead) or unresolved-rate exceeds a threshold. Do not cache None on transport/HTTP errors — cache only genuine 200-with-no-result. Persist data/geocode_cache.json with actions/cache to stop re-paying lookups, and give rescue items a retry counter (e.g. give up after 5 attempts and mark geocode_method='rescue_exhausted' so the backlog is visibly terminal, not perpetually 'in progress').

verdict.reason: Evidence verified in the actual files. geocode.py _mapbox (88-120) and _nominatim (62-82) both treat any non-200 or exception as an empty result and then unconditionally `cache[key] = result`, caching provider failure as a miss; _resolve (128-134) falls through to Nominatim indistinguishably from a genuine no-match, and geocode() never raises, so the stage cannot fail. run.py:294-295 guards the rescue pass with a bare `if MAPBOX_TOKEN:` and no else branch at all — the finding is if anything generous in saying there is a print. .gitignore contains `data/`, and CACHE_PATH is data/geocode_cache.json, so the cache is empty on every GitHub Actions run and all lookups are re-paid daily. The trigger is more likely than token rotation alone: run.py:441 runs geocode at limit=1000 and the rescue pass re-queries up to another 1000 items, each fanning out to ~6 ladder variants with zero cache reuse in CI — plausibly 5-10k Mapbox calls/day against a 100k/month free tier, so quota-driven 429s arrive within weeks. Detection is genuinely absent: health.py checks db_size, queue_depth, new_stuck and publishing_alive, and publishing_alive only fires when auto-published is exactly zero, so a halving of publication volume passes silently. No geocode-method or provider-health check exists. Severity stays medium rather than high because no bad data is written (the rescue pass skips when the new confidence is not better) and the condition self-heals in CI once the token is restored — the harm is degraded publish rates and a growing review queue, not corruption.

findings.title: The self-healing retry masks chronically failing morning runs, and GitHub's 60-day inactivity rule can kill the cron entirely — both invisible to a team that stops reading failure emails
findings.evidence: daily.yml:5-6 two crons; the guard (lines 20-40) makes a skipped 15:00 retry complete as a GREEN run, so the newest run of the day in the Actions list is green even on days the morning failed — and on days the morning DID fail, the retry succeeds and the site looks fine by evening, so the only distinct signal is a daily failure email that is quickly habituated/filtered. Nothing tracks consecutive morning failures (pipeline_run has the data; nobody queries it). Separately: GitHub disables `schedule` triggers after 60 days without repo activity — this repo's stated goal is near-zero human involvement, i.e. commits will stop.
findings.failure_scenario: Morning collect slowly outgrows the 330-min timeout (3 states, 146 districts, Google throttling): every day a red run at ~10 IST and a green retry finishing ~19 IST. Data freshness silently degrades from 'by morning' to 'by evening'; failure emails become wallpaper within a week. The day the retry ALSO fails, that email looks like all the others — zero-data days start passing unnoticed. Worst case: 60 days after the last commit, GitHub disables the schedule; one easily-missed email, then the pipeline simply stops — no runs, no failures, nothing. Time to notice: indefinite; likely when an outsider mentions the site is stale.
findings.fix: 1) Make the retry announce itself: in the guard step, when go==yes on the 09:30 UTC cron (meaning the morning failed), curl the Slack webhook with 'morning run failed — retry executing'. 2) Add a consecutive-failure canary: query pipeline_run for the last 3 morning-slot runs and alert at >=3 failures. 3) Add an external dead-man's switch: curl a healthchecks.io (or similar) ping URL as the final step of a successful daily run — silence for 36h pages the team regardless of GitHub's state, which also covers the 60-day auto-disable. 4) Optionally a monthly keepalive workflow that re-enables daily.yml via `gh api .../enable` or pushes a heartbeat commit.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified in code. The guard (daily.yml:20-40) gates every subsequent step on go=='yes', so a skipped retry completes with zero failed steps — a GREEN run — confirming the claim that the day's newest run reads green even when the morning failed. No consecutive-failure detection exists anywhere: health.py checks only in-DB resource metrics (db size, queue depth, publishing_alive) and, decisively, runs as a pipeline stage (run.py: stage("health", health.run)), so the only watchdog is inside the thing being watched and cannot fire when the run doesn't happen. The 60-day exposure is also real: grep confirms no git push/commit in .github/ — the pipeline writes to Supabase and deploys to Vercel but never touches the repo, so nothing automated resets GitHub's scheduled-workflow inactivity timer. Two caveats that reduce but don't refute it: (1) the public site renders meta.generated_at (App.jsx:177,286), so staleness is passively visible — but as an indicator nobody is required to look at, not an alert; (2) the finding's "stated goal is near-zero human involvement" is not stated in the repo (grep found nothing) and the repo is currently very active (11 commit-days since 4 Jul), so a 60-day gap is not imminent. The specific 330-min-timeout trigger is speculative given the headroom, but the finding doesn't rest on it — the repo's own comments document recurring morning-failure causes (Supabase disk-full 18 Jul, adjudicator freeze 11-14 Jul, run #9 stale site) that produce identical masking. Medium is correct: data still lands via the retry, the site shows a date, and GitHub emails before disabling — this is a detection-latency and freshness-degradation issue, not a silent outage on day one.

findings.title: Incident dedup merges distinct crashes that share a centroid geocode (distance = 0 for every crash in the same city/district)
findings.evidence: pipeline/processing/dedup.py:38-56 find_pairs requires only 'a.geom is not null ... ST_DWithin(a.geom, b.geom, 1000)' — no floor on geocode_confidence or geocode_method. geocode.py:191-193 pins city-level geocodes (conf 0.50) and district-level geocodes (conf 0.40) to one exact cached point per city/district, so every centroid-geocoded crash in the same city/district is 0 m from every other. The docstring's safety claim ('Undated or ungeocoded incidents never auto-merge') does not cover centroid-geocoded incidents. merge_incident (dedup.py:59-83) then DELETEs the losing incident row outright.
findings.failure_scenario: Bihar/UP/Rajasthan (the configured daily states) routinely produce several unrelated 1-fatality crashes in the same district within a day. Two of them extract with only city/district-level locations, both geocode to the identical centroid point, crash_date within ±1 day, |Δfatalities| ≤ 1 (trivially true for the dominant 1-dead/0-dead classes) — is_same_crash returns True and one real crash is deleted from the database. Its casualties vanish from hotspot sums and the ≥3-in-6-months escalation counter silently undercounts; the loss is unrecoverable except via the review_action before_json blob. This is the incident-level analog of the article-level global-simhash collapse that scripts/repair_false_dedup.py was written to repair.
findings.fix: In find_pairs, require point-quality geocodes on BOTH sides before auto-merging: geocode_confidence >= 0.6 (or geocode_method not like '%centroid%') and additionally reject pairs where ST_Distance = 0 AND geocode_method is a centroid method. Centroid-pinned candidates should be routed to the review console as suggested merges, mirroring the existing rule for undated/ungeocoded incidents.

verdict.reason: Evidence checks out on every point. dedup.py:33-56 find_pairs filters only on non-null crash_date, date window, non-null geom and ST_DWithin 1000m — no geocode_confidence or geocode_method predicate, and is_same_crash adds none. geocode.py:192-194 emits city_centroid (0.50) and district_centroid (0.40) from query strings that are deterministic functions of city/district/state, resolved through a persistent file cache (data/geocode_cache.json), so every centroid-geocoded incident in the same city/district lands on the identical point and ST_Distance is exactly 0. run.py:270-273 writes geom at any confidence, so those rows are in dedup scope, and merge_incident (dedup.py:78) hard-DELETEs the loser. The contrast is decisive: cluster.py:4-7 documents this exact hazard and enforces MIN_GEOCODE_CONF = 0.5 ("District-centroid geocodes (0.4) would pile up at one fake point"), while the destructive dedup path has no such floor; the docstring's safety claim covers undated/ungeocoded only. Plausibility confirmed empirically: in the 201-incident published export spanning ~2 months, 8 same-district pairs already satisfy date ±1 / |Δfat|<=1 / |Δinj|<=3 (Munger, Agra x6, Gaya); they survived only because road-level geocodes are >1000m apart — centroid geocodes force that distance to 0, so any such pair auto-merges. Over 6 months across Bihar/UP/Rajasthan this fires. Downgrading high to medium: centroid rows are below geocode_confidence_min 0.6 so they are needs_human and never published (public data is not falsified); 0.40 district centroids are already excluded from clustering so those merges do not move hotspot sums, leaving only 0.50 city centroids affecting hotspot totals and the 3-in-6-months escalation counter; and the loss is recoverable because review_action.before_json stores the full row_to_json of the deleted incident. Fix is a one-line confidence/method predicate in find_pairs.

findings.title: Rejected incidents keep their cluster_id and keep feeding hotspot scores, escalation flags, and the exported score breakdown
findings.evidence: pipeline/processing/cluster.py:27-34 clusters every incident with geom and geocode_confidence >= 0.5 — no verification_status filter; score.py:76-96 aggregates 'from incident i where i.cluster_id = %s' — also no status filter. So incidents adjudicated 'rejected' by auto_review (not a road crash: building collapse, crime, wrong country — auto_review.py:77-81) still count in incident_count, fatality/injury sums, inc_6mo, vulnerable_share and escalation_candidate. export_public.py:59 ships the full score_breakdown (including these raw sums) in the public geojson for any hotspot with ≥1 public member.
findings.failure_scenario: A hospital-ceiling-collapse article (the exact past-bug class) is extracted with 4 fatalities, geocodes fine, then gets 'rejected' by the auto-reviewer. It clusters into a hotspot that also has one legitimate public incident. The public hotspot's priority score, escalation flag, first/last crash dates and the exported breakdown raw numbers are driven partly by a record the system itself ruled out — a reviewer's rejection does not actually remove the record's influence anywhere except the incident list.
findings.fix: Filter clustering and scoring to verification_status <> 'rejected' (and decide explicitly whether 'disputed' should count). Simplest: add the status predicate to the cluster.py pts CTE and to both aggregate queries in score.py, and null out cluster_id when a status flips to rejected so the next recompute drops it.

verdict.reason: Evidence checks out line-for-line. cluster.py:27-34 selects on geom + geocode_confidence only, with no verification_status filter, and line 92 assigns cluster_id to every member. score.py:76-96 aggregates fatalities, injuries, inc_6mo, max(crash_date), vulnerable_share, geocode_confidence, source count and max defect severity purely on i.cluster_id, so rejected records drive priority_score, tier and escalation_candidate (line 104). Rejection is status-only: review/app.py:288 and auto_review.py:172 set verification_status='rejected' without clearing cluster_id or geom, so a reviewer's rejection removes influence nowhere except the incident list. migrations/003_public_views.sql:38-47 recomputes only n_public_incidents/public_fatalities/public_injuries over public members; h.* passes priority_score, score_breakdown, escalation_candidate, first_crash_date and last_crash_date through unfiltered, and export_public.py:44-60 ships all of those publicly for any hotspot with one public member. The scenario class is real and precedented: auto_review.py:77-81 explicitly rejects building/ceiling collapses, and migrations/010 documents 13 such rows already leaking once. Only nuance: 'machine_ok' crash-only records counting toward frequency is intentional by design, and the public headline incident/fatality counts are correctly filtered, so the corruption is confined to score, tier, escalation flag, first/last dates and the exported breakdown raw block — which matches medium, not high.

findings.title: city_centroid geocodes (conf 0.50) pass the >= 0.5 cluster filter — phantom mega-hotspot at each city's centroid
findings.evidence: cluster.py:17 MIN_GEOCODE_CONF = 0.5 with an inclusive '>=' at line 31; geocode.py:191 assigns city-level geocodes exactly 0.50. The module docstring says centroid geocodes 'would pile up at one fake point and manufacture phantom hotspots' but only excludes the 0.4 district tier — the 0.5 city tier is admitted by one hundredth of the boundary. All city-centroid pins in a city are the identical cached point, so DBSCAN (minpoints=1) makes them one cluster. Exported incidents.json already shows 3 public city_centroid incidents.
findings.failure_scenario: Ten unrelated crashes across Patna extract with only 'Patna' as location; all pin at the identical city-centroid coordinate and form one hotspot with incident_count 10 and an escalation flag. If any single genuinely-located public incident falls within ~237 m of the centroid, the phantom hotspot becomes publicly visible with a score, date range, and dominant defects manufactured from crashes that happened kilometres apart.
findings.fix: Raise MIN_GEOCODE_CONF above 0.5 (e.g. 0.55) or exclude geocode_method like '%centroid%' from clustering — matching the stated design intent. If city-level counting is wanted for statistics, keep those incidents cluster_id = null and aggregate them in a separate district/city table, never as a point hotspot.

verdict.reason: Mechanism verified in code. geocode.py:191 assigns city_centroid exactly 0.50 and cluster.py:31 admits it via an inclusive >= against MIN_GEOCODE_CONF = 0.5 (cluster.py:17), while the module docstring's phantom-hotspot rationale addresses only the 0.4 district tier — a genuine intent/threshold mismatch. Same-city centroid queries share one geocode cache key so every such pin is the identical coordinate, and with minpoints := 1 they deterministically form one cluster. The consequential part holds: cluster.py aggregates dominant_defects and min/max(crash_date), and score.py aggregates inc_6mo, escalation_candidate, priority_score and avg_geocode_conf, all over ALL cluster members (where i.cluster_id = hid), and export_public.py ships those fields for any hotspot with at least one public member. Live proof in web/public/data/hotspots.geojson: hotspot 81 (Jaipur) publishes score 88.9, escalation True, inc_6mo 4 with only 2 public incidents and avg_geocode_conf 0.683, i.e. a 0.5 centroid member is inside it. Two supporting details in the finding are wrong and should be corrected, but do not refute it: (1) incident_count 10 would NOT publish — migrations/003_public_views.sql:38 recomputes n_public_incidents/public_fatalities/public_injuries over public members only, and that is what the export ships; (2) the 3 public city_centroid incidents in incidents.json (ids 131, 5, 128, all conf 0.5) are public via the verification_status in ('reviewed','verified') reviewer-override branch of public_incident, not via the cluster filter, so they are not evidence of the >=0.5 leak. Net: the phantom-hotspot mechanism is real and already contaminating published scores, escalation flags, date ranges and dominant defects; only the casualty/incident counts are protected.

findings.title: Hotspot stable-matching has no claimed-set: two new clusters can capture the same hotspot id, silently merging distinct junctions and enabling centroid drift
findings.evidence: cluster.py:66-92: for each DBSCAN cluster, the code picks the nearest existing hotspot within STABLE_MATCH_M (300 m) and updates it — but never records which hotspot ids have already been claimed this rebuild. The lookup also reads centroid_geom live, i.e. values already overwritten by earlier iterations of the same loop. Additionally line 24 collapses the per-road-type epsilon config (urban 150 m … NH 300 m) into one mean (~237 m) applied everywhere.
findings.failure_scenario: Two junctions ~400 m apart are correctly separated by DBSCAN, but both centroids lie within 300 m of one old hotspot. Cluster A updates the hotspot; cluster B matches the same (now moved) row and overwrites A's stats; both clusters' incidents get the same cluster_id. The next score run scores the union — two distinct junctions permanently fused under one id, with the map pin at neither. Repeated across nightly runs the hotspot centroid can also 'walk' up to 300 m per run, dragging its stable id (and its status/authority history) to a different physical location, while urban junctions 150-237 m apart are chained together by the averaged epsilon.
findings.fix: Track claimed hotspot ids during the rebuild (skip already-claimed ones, order candidate matches by distance globally, create a new hotspot for the loser), snapshot old centroids before the loop instead of re-querying the mutating table, and either run DBSCAN per road-type epsilon group or use the minimum (150 m) in dense-urban states rather than the mean.

verdict.reason: Verified in pipeline/processing/cluster.py. The stable-match query (lines 67-71) selects the nearest hotspot within STABLE_MATCH_M with no claimed-set, no exclusion of ids already matched this rebuild, and no dedup pass afterwards; it reads the hotspot table live while line 75-81 mutates centroid_geom inside the same loop, so later iterations match against centroids already moved by earlier ones. Line 92 then stamps the same hid onto the second cluster's incidents, fusing two DBSCAN-distinct clusters under one hotspot id while incident_count/fatality_count retain only the last writer's values — an internally inconsistent row. Because minpoints=1 makes clusters single-linkage chains at eps, two clusters need only >231 m separation while both centroids sit within 300 m of one old hotspot (e.g. 250 m either side) — an ordinary geometry for adjacent urban junctions in Indian districts, not a contrived one. No test covers clustering (tests/test_core_logic.py has none). Line 24 does collapse the per-road-type config (config/config_settings.json:40-48, urban 150 … NH 300) into a single mean; the exact value is 231 m, not the ~237 m claimed, and the module docstring says the pass runs at "the modal epsilon 250 m", so the code contradicts its own documented decision. That arithmetic slip is the only inaccuracy and does not affect the finding. Severity medium is right: silent and recurring, and it breaks the stable identity that carries hotspot status and authority-escalation history, but it is repairable by a rebuild once matching is fixed.

findings.title: Watch-site matching corroborates generic names with the site's own district tag (circular), and geo-matches centroid-quality pins
findings.evidence: watch.py:71-75 collect_sites stamps every article found by a site's Google News query with that site's state/district. watch.py:35-37 name_matches then accepts 'district.lower() == (article_district or '').lower()' as locality corroboration — for watch-collected articles this compares the site's district to itself. The docstring claims matching is 'conjunctive to survive generic names', but the conjunct is self-supplied. Substring checks also lack word boundaries (line 30-34: city 'Agra' matches inside 'agriculture', 'Una' inside 'unaware'). The geo pass (watch.py:108-117) joins any incident geom within 500 m with no geocode_confidence/method filter, so 0.4-0.5 centroid pins (which land at administrative centres, where audited junctions typically are) trigger 'incident within Xm of <site>' hits.
findings.failure_scenario: Site 'Medical College Junction, Gorakhpur': the watch query returns a story about Patna's Medical College Junction; the article is stamped district=Gorakhpur at insert, the variant matches the text, the circular district check passes, and a Slack alert claims activity at the audited Gorakhpur junction — the alert that CFI's authority-complaint follow-ups are built on. Separately, any city-centroid-geocoded crash in the same city as a watched central junction fires a geo hit for a crash that may have happened 10 km away.
findings.fix: For articles inserted by collect_sites, require corroboration from the article TEXT only (city or district string present in text), not the collector tag; use word-boundary regex for city/variant matching; and add geocode_confidence >= 0.6 (or method not like '%centroid%') to the geo-pass join.

verdict.reason: Both core claims verified in source. (1) Circular district corroboration: watch.py:71-75 stamps every watch-collected article with the site's own district at insert; name_matches (watch.py:35-37) accepts `district.lower() == (article_district or '').lower()` as locality corroboration, so for those articles the conjunct is self-supplied and the docstring's generic-name guarantee (lines 12-14) is void. tests/test_core_logic.py:101 encodes this as the expected pass, on the very case lines 97-98 declare must fail. (2) Geo pass has no geocode_confidence filter: watch.py:108-117 joins any incident geom within 500m. geocode.py:191-193 sets city_centroid=0.50 and district_centroid=0.40, and cluster.py:4-6 / MIN_GEOCODE_CONF=0.5 explicitly excludes exactly these as 'phantom' points; run.py:304 treats <0.6 as needing rescue. The watch geo pass is the sole consumer that trusts them, and centroids resolve to administrative centres where audited central junctions sit, making sub-500m false hits structurally likely rather than rare. (3) Substring checks at lines 30-34 do lack word boundaries — accurate but only a contributing factor since a variant must also match. Severity medium is right: no public publish path (watch_hit feeds only the Slack digest at watch.py:141-148 and the review console, with a human reading the linked source), which caps impact, but the alert asserts a specific factual claim used to reopen authority complaints, and the geo pass silently reverses a filter the repo documents as necessary.

findings.title: Hotspot rows are never deleted — stale/orphaned hotspots accumulate and are re-scored every night forever
findings.evidence: cluster.py creates hotspots (line 84-91) and updates matched ones (75-81), but has no deletion path for hotspots whose incidents merged away (dedup.py:77 deletes incidents), moved clusters, or whose centroid drifted >300m (a NEW row is created, cluster.py:12, leaving the old one orphaned with stale counts). score.py:70-72 selects `select id from hotspot` and runs its 3-query scoring loop over EVERY hotspot nightly, including orphans whose member count is now 0. The public view hides memberless hotspots (003_public_views.sql:38-47), so the growth is invisible on the site but real in the table and the nightly loop.
findings.failure_scenario: Slow leak: every centroid drift or merge leaves a permanent orphan row carrying stale incident_count/fatality_count. Over a year this is hundreds-to-thousands of dead rows, each costing ~3 queries + 1 jsonb UPDATE per night in score.py (compounding finding #3's O(N) recompute), and any future internal query that reads hotspot.incident_count directly (rather than the public view) reports stale numbers.
findings.fix: At the end of cluster.run(), delete or flag orphans: `delete from hotspot h where not exists (select 1 from incident i where i.cluster_id = h.id)` — safe because incident.cluster_id FK is `on delete set null` and status history worth keeping (escalated_to_govt etc.) can be exempted with `and h.status = 'new'`; audit-log the deletions to review_action.

verdict.reason: All evidence verified in code: cluster.py inserts (84-91) and updates (75-81) hotspots but has no delete path; a >300m centroid drift or cluster merge creates a new row and reassigns incidents (line 92), permanently orphaning the old row with stale counts. dedup.py:77 hard-deletes merged incidents (FK is incident-side 'on delete set null', never touching hotspot). score.py:70 loops over every hotspot id nightly with 2 SELECTs + 1 jsonb UPDATE each, including zero-member orphans. public_hotspot (003_public_views.sql:38-47) hides memberless rows, making growth invisible publicly, while run.py:364-374's internal TOP HOTSPOTS query reads stale hotspot.incident_count directly. Repo-wide grep confirms no cleanup/prune anywhere. Minor mitigation: the 300m stable-match can re-adopt an orphan near a future centroid, but this doesn't bound growth. Impact is a slow leak with trivial nightly cost, so low severity is right.

findings.title: VERCEL_TOKEN expiry: public site freezes; CI path is loud but the local fallback swallows it
findings.evidence: daily.yml's deploy step (`npx vercel deploy --prod --token "$VERCEL_TOKEN"`) is unguarded, so in CI an expired token fails the run → GitHub email (loud). But scripts/daily.sh — the documented local fallback — runs the deploy with `|| echo "WARN vercel deploy failed (site keeps yesterday's data)" >> "$LOG"` and exits with the PIPELINE's status, so a deploy failure never changes the exit code and only lands in an unread local log. The token (vcp_...) is in .env and GitHub secrets; Vercel tokens are commonly minted with an expiration, which cannot be verified from the repo.
findings.failure_scenario: Token expires → DB keeps getting fresh data daily but cfi-defect-repository.vercel.app freezes at the last deploy — the exact 'stale site' failure mode the repo's own run #9 postmortem calls the worst outcome. In CI it shows as a daily red run (plus the 15:00 IST retry re-running the entire ~35-min pipeline just to fail at the same last step). If ops ever falls back to the local cron, staleness is completely silent.
findings.fix: Check the vcp_ token's expiration in the Vercel dashboard now; prefer a non-expiring token or calendar the renewal. Add `vercel whoami --token` to the monthly check-secrets probes. In daily.sh, propagate deploy failure into the exit status instead of WARN-and-continue.

verdict.reason: Code evidence verified: daily.yml's deploy step (line 82) is unguarded so an expired VERCEL_TOKEN fails the run loudly, and scripts/daily.sh (lines 14-17, 22) does swallow deploy failures via `|| echo WARN >> $LOG` while exiting with the pipeline's status. Token (vcp_...) confirmed in .env. However, the silent-staleness scenario is dormant: `crontab -l` shows daily.sh is not installed locally and the pipeline has been fully cloud-autonomous via GitHub Actions since 7 Jul 2026, so the only active path fails loudly same-day (red run + email) with recovery being a simple token rotation — staleness bounded to hours. Token expiry is also unverifiable and Vercel supports non-expiring tokens. Real hygiene gap (no rotation runbook, wasted 35-min retry, swallowed error in fallback code) but the impact is a loud, quickly recoverable annoyance, not a silent freeze.

findings.title: SUPABASE_KEY: unused 10-year service_role credential replicated across three secret stores
findings.evidence: settings.py:13-14 defines SUPABASE_URL/SUPABASE_KEY but grep shows no module imports them — zero consumers. Yet .env holds a service_role JWT (iat 2026-07-04, exp 2036 — exactly 10 years), and daily.yml injects it into every pipeline run while check-secrets.yml dutifully reports it PRESENT. It is a legacy JWT-format key: rotating the project's JWT secret (a one-click Supabase action, also part of the migration to new sb_secret_ keys) kills it instantly.
findings.failure_scenario: Two-sided risk. If it dies (JWT-secret rotation), nothing breaks and check-secrets still says PRESENT — false comfort about a secret that never mattered. Until then, a full-privilege key that bypasses the RLS enabled in migration 007 sits unused in local .env, GitHub secrets, and the env of every CI run — pure blast radius with no consumer that would ever notice compromise.
findings.fix: Delete SUPABASE_KEY (and SUPABASE_URL if unused) from .env, GitHub secrets, daily.yml, check-secrets.yml, and settings.py until something actually consumes it. If Supabase API features are needed later, mint a new-format sb_secret key at that point.

verdict.reason: Every evidence claim verified against the repo: settings.py:13-14 defines SUPABASE_URL/SUPABASE_KEY and no module imports them (15 settings import sites checked, none pulls these names; no direct env access; migration 007's own comment confirms "No component uses the PostgREST Data API"). Decoded JWT confirms role=service_role, iat 2026-07-04, exp 2036-07-03 (exactly 10.0 years), legacy HS256 format killed by JWT-secret rotation. daily.yml:64 injects it into every run and check-secrets.yml:19 reports it PRESENT despite zero consumers. Genuine hygiene finding: unused full-privilege RLS-bypassing credential replicated in .env, GitHub secrets, and every CI run env, with a false-comfort presence check. Severity low is right — trivial to remove, no functional breakage either way within 6 months, risk is latent blast radius only.

findings.title: Watch Slack notify fails silently and permanently — a revoked webhook (4xx) just prints a WARN; a missing secret is a designed no-op
findings.evidence: watch.py:155-156: non-2xx from Slack -> `print WARN slack webhook returned {status}` -> return {sent:0}; the stage succeeds, ok stays True, workflow exits 0. Slack returns a permanent 404 for revoked webhooks (app uninstalled, channel deleted), so this retries and fails identically forever. watch.py:137-140: unset SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL is a 'graceful no-op' shown only on a review console nobody is required to open (Render free tier, sleeps when idle).
findings.failure_scenario: The Slack app is uninstalled or the channel archived. Junction-activity alerts — the feature's entire purpose is triggering complaint-reopening with authorities — stop arriving. The team reads silence as 'no activity at our audited junctions'. Hits keep accumulating unnotified in watch_hit. Time to notice: months, because there is no expected message cadence whose absence would be missed.
findings.fix: On non-2xx, raise (let the watch stage fail -> ok=False -> workflow failure email) or at minimum record notify_failed in the returned stats and have cmd_daily's canary check treat 'unnotified hits older than 48h' as ok=False. Add a weekly heartbeat post ('site-watch alive: N sites monitored, M hits this week — even if M=0') so silence itself becomes detectable. Surface 'oldest unnotified watch_hit age' on /qa.

verdict.reason: Evidence verified as accurate. /Users/a39002/Documents/Claude/crashfree-infra-repo/pipeline/processing/watch.py:155-156 does exactly what is claimed: a non-2xx from the webhook only does `print(f"  WARN slack webhook returned {r.status_code}")` and returns `{"pending": len(hits), "sent": 0}`. Confirmed at /Users/a39002/Documents/Claude/crashfree-infra-repo/pipeline/run.py:391-442 that the `stage()` wrapper flips `ok = False` only inside an exception handler, so a returned dict — whatever it contains — leaves ok=True and the workflow exits 0. Lines 137-140 confirm the unset-secret no-op, and .github/workflows/daily.yml:66 documents it as intended ("empty = console only"). There is no alerting, no retry, no consecutive-failure counter, and no expected-cadence heartbeat anywhere, so a permanent 404 (uninstalled app, archived channel) would repeat identically and invisibly, exactly as described. Two things argue for downgrading severity rather than refuting: (1) on non-2xx the code does NOT mark hits notified, so nothing is lost — every pending hit flushes on the next run once the hook is repaired, making this a delayed-notification bug, not data loss; (2) review/app.py:207-222 renders pending watch hits on the review console, so a genuine pull-based fallback surface exists (weak, since nobody is required to open it). Probability of webhook revocation for a small nonprofit workspace inside ~6 months is real but not high. Net: a genuine silent-failure gap worth a non-2xx raise or a stale-notification check, but low severity given automatic recovery and zero data loss.

findings.title: Telemetry discards nearly all stage counts ('done' strings), so /qa — the designated alerting surface — cannot reveal any of the silent failures, and it is pull-only on a sleeping free-tier service
findings.evidence: run.py:399 `stats[name] = fn() or "done"` — cmd_collect wrapper, cmd_process, cmd_geocode, and export_main all return None, so pipeline_run.stage_stats records literally 'done' for the stages where every silent failure above lives (counts exist only in Actions stdout, which nobody reads unless already suspicious). Only watch, auto_review and hygiene return dicts. review/app.py:160-171 renders just id/started/finished/ok/note, and its own header admits the alerting model: 'ok=False means a stage failed' — i.e. detection requires a human to open a dashboard daily, hosted on Render free tier that sleeps (render.yaml).
findings.failure_scenario: Any of the degradations above (0 collected, 0 fetched, 0 geocoded, mapbox dead, 0 adjudicated) leaves a row saying ok=True, stage_stats={collect:'done',process:'done',geocode:'done',...} — the QA page shows ten green rows and a human auditing after a suspected problem still can't see WHICH day ingestion died or what the counts were. Detection latency of every other finding is multiplied because the forensic data was thrown away.
findings.fix: Make every cmd_ return its stats dict (collect totals incl. new/errors, process stats incl. failed/budget-stopped, geocode method distribution + provider outcomes, export counts) so stage_stats becomes a real time series. Render day-over-day deltas on /qa with red highlighting for zeros. Then add one push channel: a single end-of-run Slack digest line ('#412 ok=True · 37 new · 21 extracted · 14 geocoded · 6 published · $1.42') — the cheapest possible conversion of every silent failure into a visibly-missing or visibly-zero daily message.

verdict.reason:
The code-level evidence is accurate: run.py:399 `stats[name] = fn() or "done"` discards counts, and cmd_collect/cmd_process/cmd_geocode are all `-> None` (counts go to stdout only), so stage_stats stores the literal string 'done' for collect/process/geocode/recompute/export. That forensic loss is real and does mean you cannot reconstruct which day a stage degraded or by how much.

However the finding's load-bearing causal claim is REFUTED by the code. It asserts /qa is "the designated alerting surface" and that "detection requires a human to open a dashboard daily" on a sleeping Render free tier. pipeline/processing/health.py runs as a daily stage (run.py:454) and PUSHES a batched Slack alert via SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL when thresholds cross — its docstring says it exists so "cliffs announce themselves weeks early." It checks db_size, queue_depth (diverging extraction backlog), new_stuck, and publishing_alive, the last of which specifically catches the "0 adjudicated" scenario the finding names, and it does so by reading stage_stats->'auto_review'->>'auto_published' — i.e. the forensic data for that stage is retained, not thrown away. The `watch` stage also posts to Slack. Additionally /qa renders live DB aggregates (ingestion by state x language, article funnel, geocode confidence by method, hotspot statuses), not merely the id/started/finished/ok/note run table the finding describes, so a human auditing after a suspected problem has far more than "ten green rows."

So the scenario as written ("leaves a row saying ok=True ... and nobody can tell") does not hold for most of the enumerated degradations — they trip a Slack push. What genuinely survives is narrower: a TOTAL ingestion death is still silent, because queue_depth and new_stuck alert only on values being too HIGH (never zero), and publishing_alive self-excuses via the `spend < 0.10` clause when there is nothing to process. `min_extracted_last_run` is declared in health.DEFAULTS but never referenced in collect_checks(), which is the actual zero-detection gap — and that is properly a separate finding about health-check coverage, not about telemetry serialization. Downgrading to low: the defect is a forensic/debuggability gap that slows root-causing, not the absence of alerting that the finding claims.

findings.title: No hotspot retirement: dead hotspots decay in score but stay on the public map forever
findings.evidence: hotspot.status ('new'/'monitoring'/'fixed'/…) is never written by any pipeline code (grep: only the default and the review console); cluster.py only updates/creates, never archives; score.py recomputes every hotspot every night (score.py:70-71 'select id from hotspot') regardless of age; export_public.py:40-46 exports every public_hotspot with no tier, score, or last_crash_date filter. Recency decay (exp(-days/90)) floors the score into the 'watch' tier but nothing removes the dot.
findings.failure_scenario: Twelve months in, hotspots whose defect was repaired (or that were built from a single 2025 monsoon story) still render as pins with stale dominant_defects and year-old last_crash_date. The map progressively fills with dead dots, drowning the live escalation candidates and inviting the government counterpart to point at an already-fixed site to discredit the dataset. Score decay also never reaches zero, so no threshold ever naturally excludes them.
findings.fix: Add an explicit retirement rule in the nightly recompute: e.g. status -> 'monitoring'/'dormant' when last_crash_date is older than N months (config), and either exclude dormant hotspots from hotspots.geojson or export them under a separate 'archive' layer with visual de-emphasis. Keep the row (history matters for reopened complaints), just stop presenting it as live.

verdict.reason: Evidence is factually accurate on all four points, verified against code and live export data. hotspot.status is declared in migrations/001_schema.sql:108-109 with a 'fixed'/'monitoring'/'escalated_to_govt' enum but is written by zero code paths — review/app.py:158 only aggregates it for a QA table, and the live web/public/data/hotspots.geojson shows all 153 hotspots stuck at status 'new'. cluster.py only updates-or-inserts (never archives), score.py:70 recomputes every hotspot unconditionally, and export_public.py:40-46 exports all of public_hotspot with no tier/score/recency filter — public_hotspot (003_public_views.sql:38-47) gates only on 'has >=1 public member incident', which is permanent once satisfied. So a hotspot genuinely can never leave the public map, and a reviewer who learns a defect was repaired has no way to record it. However the stated harm is overstated: web/src/App.jsx already provides a priority-tier filter, tier-coloured dots, per-tier counts, a repeat-only toggle and a score-sorted Rankings view, and escalation_candidate is recomputed from a rolling 6-month window — so live candidates remain separable and are not 'drowned'. Retention is also defensible for an evidence repository where every pin carries its own last_crash_date and source URLs. The pipeline has no repair-data source, so retirement was always going to be a manual review action. findings.title: Relative crash dates resolve against UTC-rendered published_at, shifting IST publication days back one day
findings.evidence: run.py:199 passes published_at=str(a.get('published_at')) — a timestamptz that psycopg renders in the session timezone (UTC on Supabase), e.g. '2026-07-18 19:00:00+00:00' for an article published 00:30 IST on 19 Jul. extract.py:145-150 instructs the model to resolve 'yesterday'/weekday names against that string. RSS pubDates are likewise GMT (rss.py published field).
findings.failure_scenario: A crash on the night of 17 Jul is reported by outlet A at 09:00 IST 18 Jul (UTC date 18 Jul → 'yesterday' = 17 Jul, correct) and by outlet B at 01:00 IST 18 Jul (UTC date 17 Jul → 'last night' resolves to 16 Jul). The two incidents are 1 day apart and still merge, but a second shifted outlet or a 'Friday night' phrasing produces a 2-day spread that breaks the ±1-day dedup window — one real crash becomes two incidents, feeding the double-count and escalation problems above. scripts/repair_dates.py existing at all suggests date drift has already needed repair once.
findings.fix: Convert published_at to Asia/Kolkata before formatting the prompt (published_at.astimezone(ZoneInfo('Asia/Kolkata')).strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M IST (%A)')) and say explicitly that the article's local calendar day is the IST date. Including the weekday name also removes the model's need to compute it.

verdict.reason: Mechanism confirmed, stated impact refuted. Confirmed: published_at is timestamptz (migrations/001_schema.sql:15); pipeline/db.py connect() sets no session TimeZone (only statement_timeout), so psycopg renders it in the Supabase server default (UTC); run.py:199 passes that raw string into extract.py:143-147, whose prompt resolves 'yesterday'/'on Friday'/weekday names against it. Articles published 00:00-05:30 IST therefore carry a UTC date one calendar day earlier, yielding crash_date off by one day. REFUTED - the dedup-split consequence: dedup.py:22 uses abs(date delta) <= 1 day, and this shift is strictly unidirectional and bounded at exactly one day (UTC rendering can only move an IST timestamp backward, never forward). A shifted outlet and a correct outlet land at delta=1, inside tolerance, and merge. The claimed 2-day spread requires a forward shift, which this mechanism cannot produce. No incident split, no double-count, no escalation-counter inflation (score.py:78 buckets over 6 months, where one day is immaterial). Also refuted as supporting evidence: scripts/repair_dates.py documents a different, already-fixed bug - crash_date extracted with NO publication date producing wrong YEAR (query filters published_at::date - crash_date > 30), not timezone drift. What survives is a genuine but minor data-integrity defect: one-day date imprecision on the subset of incidents sourced from early-morning-IST articles using relative dating. Cheap fix (add -c TimeZone=Asia/Kolkata to the psycopg options string, or format IST-aware at the call site). Severity stays low.

refuted.title: Geocode cache is gitignored, so every GitHub Actions run starts cold — the daily 'rescue pass' re-fires the same Mapbox/Nominatim queries every day, walking straight into the Mapbox 100k/mo cliff
refuted.reason: The mechanical evidence is accurate (data/ is gitignored, daily.yml does a bare checkout with no actions/cache so CI starts cache-cold; _mapbox treats any non-200 as a silent miss with no 402/429 handling; the rescue query has no attempt counter) — but the quota-cliff scenario's engine is empirically false. The claim requires a 400-500-item stuck-below-0.6 queue that is 're-selected forever' and 'only grows'. Production DB after ~3 weeks and 1,084 incidents shows the rescue queue is ZERO (and geom-null is zero): auto_review.py adjudicates every 'auto' incident daily into terminal statuses (auto_published/rejected/machine_ok) or needs_human, and the rescue query only selects ('auto','needs_human'). All 60 remaining low-confidence incidents sit in machine_ok — permanently outside rescue scope; the 13 needs_human items all have geocode_confidence >= 0.6. So the daily rescue pass currently re-fires ~0 Mapbox queries, not thousands. Realistic volume: ~285 new incidents/week x ~4-6 ladder variants ~= 8-11k Mapbox requests/month, an order of magnitude under the 100k cliff; incident creation is capped by the $2/day LLM budget, so even 3-5x state expansion within 6 months stays ~25-40k/month. Also the second cron is a skip-if-today-succeeded retry, so it is ~1 run/day, not 2. Residual truth (cold cache wastes some free-tier requests; no Mapbox usage alerting) is a low-grade hygiene gap, not a high-severity quota cliff within 6 months.

refuted.title: Vercel Hobby bandwidth: the dashboard ships the entire unbounded incidents.json + hotspots.geojson to every visitor — already 477KB at pilot scale with only a 300s cache, on a plan capped at 100GB/mo and licensed for non-commercial use
refuted.reason: Evidence partially checks out (unbounded full-corpus export in export_public.py:65-91, fetches in App.jsx:30-32, 300s cache, raw sizes 322KB+155KB) but the failure scenario collapses under verified numbers. (1) The finding claims ~10 public incidents; meta.json shows 201 incidents / 153 hotspots across 8 states — so per-incident weight is ~1.6KB raw and the projected 5-10MB payload needs 3,000-6,000 incidents, while actual growth is ~5 incidents/day (52 in first 10 days of July), i.e. ~1,100 incidents (~1.8MB raw) in 6 months even before any cap. (2) It ignores compression: Vercel serves JSON gzip/brotli and bills transferred bytes; the real payload gzips to ~78KB today (66.6KB + 11.7KB, measured), and even the scenario's 5-10MB raw is ~1-2MB transferred. Recomputed worst case (3x growth + bundle) ≈ 1.4MB/visit; a 20k-visit press spike ≈ 28GB, well under the 100GB/mo cap — breaching it needs ~70-100k+ visits/month, implausible within 6 months. (3) The 300s TTL doesn't affect Vercel's transfer metering for distinct visitors. (4) The Hobby non-commercial-terms exposure is unverified (plan not determinable from repo) and is a with-notice upgrade request, not a cliff. The underlying no-pagination design is true but does not bite within the ~6-month horizon.

refuted.title: Unbounded daily re-geocoding: 'geom is null' set and rescue set grow forever, no attempt marker, no ORDER BY
refuted.reason: Evidence quotes are accurate (no ORDER BY, no attempt marker, limit=1000, 330-min timeout, cold CI cache), but the scenario's core premise is false. The geocode ladder always ends with a "{district} district, {state}" centroid variant (geocode.py:192-193, conf 0.40), and run.py:257-259 coalesces district/state from the source article, which the district-based collector always knows — so nearly every incident resolves on first attempt, sets geom, and permanently exits the 'geom is null' set. Production DB confirms: 0 of 1,084 incidents have null geom after ~6 weeks of daily cloud runs (claimed growth was 10-30/day; actual is 0/day). The rescue set is likewise empty (0 rows): auto_review adjudicates every 'auto' item exactly once and routes the bulk to terminal statuses that exit the set (machine_ok 548 incl. all crash-only regardless of geocode, auto_published 410, rejected 93); all 77 sub-0.6-confidence incidents sit in terminal statuses, and the 13 needs_human items all have conf >= 0.6. With ~0/day accumulation in both sets, limit-1000 saturation, publication starvation, and the 6-12k-requests/day timeout creep are implausible within 6 months. The missing attempt-marker/ORDER BY is at most a hygiene note, not a high-severity ops risk.

refuted.title: review_action audit log is append-only with fat jsonb payloads and no retention — several rows per incident per lifetime, including full-row before_json snapshots
refuted.reason: Evidence is mechanically accurate (all four writer sites confirmed; no retention anywhere; hygiene purges only raw_html), but the growth scenario is implausible within 6 months at realistic volume. Live data shows ~54 incidents total after weeks at the 3-state scope (the 49-incident figure was a one-time bulk run), so steady state is ~5-25 incidents/day. Audit rows are mostly 200-500B (verdict jsonb has 6 short fields, notes truncated to 150 chars); the fat ~1-2.5KB before_json merge rows are rare (1 merge per ~50 incidents in live data). Realistic growth is ~10-50KB/day → 2-9MB in 6 months (~1-2% of the 400MB health alert), not 50-200KB/day. Rows per incident are bounded one-shot per stage (adjudicate-once flips to needs_human; rescue re-queue requires strict geocode improvement crossing 0.6, then leaves the predicate). And the audit log can never be the marginal quota contributor: each incident's ~1KB of audit rows ships with 5-20KB of clean_text/translated_text in source_article that scales by the same multiplier if ingestion widens — the article tables trip the alert first (as raw_html already did, covered by finding #5). Append-only is also deliberate design (auditability principle in CLAUDE.md and code docstrings), and a retention line in the existing hygiene stage is a trivial future one-liner.

refuted.title: Hygiene raw_html purge is one unbatched UPDATE — after any backlog day it rewrites GBs in a single transaction, the exact WAL/disk-spike class that caused the 18 Jul outage
refuted.reason: Evidence is wrong on the load-bearing details. (1) The quoted SQL does not exist: run.py:450-451 is `update source_article set raw_html = null where raw_html is not null` with no processing_status filter, so the claimed trigger (thousands of articles flipping to terminal status) has no effect on what the purge touches. (2) raw_html is never stored: every insert path hard-codes raw_html=None (run.py:56, 75, 101; watch.py:76), with an explicit comment (run.py:71-74) that this was the fix for the 18 Jul outage. The hygiene UPDATE is a self-described belt-and-suspenders no-op matching ~0 rows. (3) repair_false_dedup.py:86 only resets processing_status to 'fetched'; it never writes raw_html, so backlog reprocessing cannot create the GB-scale heap. The only raw_html writer is the one-off manual scripts/import_jsonl.py. (4) Because hygiene runs daily, even a storage regression bounds accumulation to one day's ingest, and health.py alerts at 400MB DB size long before GB scale. The 300KB/page and 1.5GB figures come from a historical post-mortem comment describing pre-fix behavior, not current growth.

refuted.title: The diverging fetched backlog carries 948 MB of raw_html (64% of the whole 1.48 GB database) — queue growth is also storage growth toward a Supabase quota kill
refuted.reason: Already fixed in code and refuted by live DB. The hygiene stage (run.py:450-451) purges raw_html UNCONDITIONALLY — no terminal-status filter as claimed — and raw_html is never stored at all: every insert path hard-codes raw_html=None (run.py:56/75/101, watch.py:76) per commits cf2e6e5/fe10d91 which fixed the very quota incident the finding cites. Live Supabase measurement: 0 rows with raw_html (0 bytes, not 948 MB), DB is 68 MB total (not 1.48 GB), source_article is 42 MB (not 1,459 MB). The 3,158 fetched-backlog rows hold only clean_text, so the 120 MB/day quota-kill scenario has no basis.

refuted.title: db.py statement_timeout=120s: full-table operations on source_article already exceed it, and the nightly dedup self-join/cluster window queries will start getting cancelled as incidents grow
refuted.reason: Evidence is partly correct but the scenario is not plausible. The timeout is real (db.py:10) and dedup/cluster are the queries named, but (a) dedup.find_pairs uses ST_DWithin against idx_incident_geom (migrations/001_schema.sql:63, GiST) plus idx_incident_date, so it is index-driven, not an O(n^2) scan; (b) cluster.run's N+1 queries are per-statement `where id = any(...)` against the PK and idx_incident_defect_incident, each with its own fresh 120s budget; (c) scale is 54 incidents today (README.md:277), largest run 49 incidents — six months of growth lands around 5-10k, and the finding's own trigger of 50-100k is years away and would probably still clear 120s on indexed plans. The supporting anecdote is also misattributed: the cancelled query scanned source_article.raw_html, a column the pipeline deliberately never writes (run.py:71, watch.py:76) and nulls+VACUUMs nightly (run.py:445-458), on a table dedup/cluster never touch. Adjacent, genuinely plausible but distinct issue: `vacuum source_article` in _hygiene (run.py:453-455) runs under the same 120s timeout on the table that actually grows fast — different query, different failure mode (disk bloat, not frozen hotspot layers).

refuted.title: Adjudication starvation (budget or Anthropic monthly limit) still produces zero alerts — the 11-14 Jul frozen-map incident would be silent again today
refuted.reason:
The load-bearing evidence claim — "detection was never added: nothing anywhere evaluates reviewed==0 or auto_published==0" — is factually wrong. /Users/a39002/Documents/Claude/crashfree-infra-repo/pipeline/processing/health.py implements exactly that check, and its comment names the incident: `("publishing_alive", pub > 0 or spend < 0.10, "last run auto-published {pub} (spend ${spend}) — 0 published at real spend means the adjudicator is starved")`, reading `stage_stats->'auto_review'->>'auto_published'` off the last completed pipeline_run. It is wired in as a daily stage (run.py `stage("health", health.run)`) and any failed check posts a batched Slack alert via SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL. The same module also covers the chronic-backlog variant with `queue_depth` (alert at 4000 'fetched', configured in config/config_settings.json:78, with the comment "diverging queue means the daily budget can't keep up") and `new_stuck` at 15000. So the claimed scenario — "every daily run stays green, zero alerts, map frozen for days to weeks" — is refuted for the budget-starvation cause that actually caused 11-14 Jul: adjudication spends real money, publishes 0, and publishing_alive fires the next run.

Residual gaps exist but are narrower and lower-severity than the finding states, and they are not what it argued: (1) the `or spend < 0.10` escape means a total API death (Anthropic monthly limit, where every call raises and run spend ≈ $0) suppresses publishing_alive — that specific sub-case falls back on queue_depth at 4000, which is slower; (2) health reads the last run with `ok is not null`, so the current run's own stats aren't visible and detection lags one run (~1 day, not weeks); (3) the run.py:421-424 baseline query `coalesce(sum((stage_stats->>'llm_spend_usd')::numeric),0)` does skip a crashed morning run whose stage_stats is NULL, so a retry could get a fresh $1.95 — accurate, but the blast radius is one extra day's cap (~$2), and every stage is individually try/excepted so a crash before the final update requires an out-of-band kill. A tightened version of gap (1) would be a legitimate medium finding; the finding as written is not real.

refuted.title: No URL canonicalization: AMP/mobile/tracking variants of one story dodge seen_url, and the simhash net has 7-day + locality holes
refuted.reason: Evidence is factually accurate about the code (no URL canonicalization; seen_url is exact-match; near_duplicate is 7-day + same-district scoped and fails open on null locality), but both routes to the claimed harm are closed. (1) The GDELT path cited as the null-locality carrier never produces incidents: run.py:97-103 inserts processing_status='new' with clean_text=None, and the only article consumer is cmd_process reading articles_by_status('fetched') (run.py:143, the sole call site in the repo). Nothing promotes 'new'->'fetched', so the fail-open branch at store.py:139-141 is unreachable on any incident-creating path. The RSS path, the only one that creates incidents, always supplies district+state from the config spine (run.py:65), so locality is never null there. (2) The 7-day simhash window is shadowed by the daily cron's 2-day RSS collection window (run.py:512, --days default=2) — a story resurfacing after >7 days is outside the feed window that would re-surface it. (3) Incident-level dedup is an effective backstop: config_settings.json sets spatial_window_m=1000, date_window_days=1, and two copies of one story carry near-identical text, hence near-identical location_text_best, hence the same geocode pin (~0m apart) — is_same_crash (dedup.py:17-31) merges them. Missing utm_*/amp//m. normalization is a real but redundant hardening gap behind two working guards, not a live duplicate-incident or spurious-escalation risk within six months. The cited Gilat 2-Bhaskar-URL case would be caught by same-district simhash inside the 2-day window.
